What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

What $10,000 grows to at different rates over 30 years — the rate difference matters more than you think.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Future value (FV) is the projected worth of an investment at a specific point in the future, based on an assumed rate of growth. It answers the most practical question in investing: "If I invest this money today, what will it be worth in 10, 20, or 30 years?"

Future value calculations rest on compound interest — the principle that your returns earn their own returns over time. Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest "the eighth wonder of the world," and while the attribution is debatable, the math is not. The difference between simple interest (returns on your original investment only) and compound interest (returns on your investment plus accumulated returns) becomes enormous over long time horizons.

The basic future value formula for a lump sum investment is:

For example, $10,000 invested at 8% for 20 years:

FV = $10,000 x (1.08)^20 = $10,000 x 4.661 = $46,610

The table reveals two critical insights. First, small differences in return rates produce massive differences over long periods — $10,000 at 6% grows to $57,435 over 30 years, while the same amount at 10% grows to $174,494. That 4-percentage-point difference triples the outcome. Second, time is the dominant variable. At 8%, your money doubles roughly every 9 years — so 30 years gives you more than three doublings, turning $10,000 into over $100,000.

Most people do not invest a single lump sum and walk away. They invest regularly — monthly or per paycheck — over decades. The future value of a series of regular contributions uses a different formula called the future value of an annuity:

Where PMT is the periodic contribution, r is the periodic rate, and n is the total number of periods.

In practice, you do not need to calculate this by hand. The insight that matters is this: regular contributions are far more powerful than most people realize because each contribution starts its own compounding clock. Your first $500 contribution compounds for the full 30 years, while your 360th contribution (at month 360) compounds for just one month — but together they build wealth that dwarfs a single lump sum.

A person investing $500 per month at 8% for 30 years accumulates $745,180 — from total contributions of only $180,000. That means $565,180, or 76% of the final balance, came from compound returns rather than your own deposits. This is the engine of wealth building.

Every future value calculation should be done twice — once in nominal terms and once in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. The nominal return is the raw number your investments earn. The real return subtracts inflation, showing you what your money will actually buy.

Historically, the S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% nominally and 7% after inflation. The difference matters enormously over long periods:

That $1.13 million in nominal terms has the purchasing power of roughly $610,000 in today's dollars — still excellent, but nearly half less than the headline number suggests. When planning for FI, always use real returns (6-7%) rather than nominal returns (9-10%) to avoid overestimating what your portfolio will actually support in retirement spending.

The Rule of 72 is the simplest and most useful mental math tool in investing. Divide 72 by your annual rate of return to estimate how many years it takes for your investment to double:

This works in reverse too. If you want to know what rate of return you need to double your money in 15 years: 72 / 15 = 4.8%. The Rule of 72 is an approximation — it is most accurate for rates between 5% and 12% — but it is remarkably precise within that range and far faster than pulling out a calculator.

The FI community uses future value calculations as the backbone of retirement planning. The process works in three steps:

The table shows how starting balance and monthly contribution interact. Notice that increasing your monthly contribution from $1,500 to $2,500 (a $1,000 increase) with a $100,000 starting balance cuts 3.5 years off your time to $1 million. This is the savings rate lever in action — the amount you save each month matters more than any other variable you control.

A common question is whether it is better to invest a lump sum now or spread contributions over time (dollar-cost averaging). The math is clear: lump sum investing wins approximately two-thirds of the time because markets trend upward over the long term. However, dollar-cost averaging reduces the psychological risk of investing a large amount right before a downturn and provides a behavioral advantage that keeps many investors on track. For most FI-seekers, the question is academic — you invest each paycheck as it arrives because you do not have a large lump sum sitting on the sidelines.

Planning with real returns ensures you are targeting a portfolio that can actually support your desired spending level.

Track your actual spending for 3 months and annualize it. Multiply by 25 to get your FI number using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. If you spend $60,000 per year, your FI number is $1,500,000.

Add up all retirement accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), taxable brokerage accounts, and savings. Exclude home equity and non-liquid assets. This is your starting balance for the future value calculation.

Subtract your monthly spending from your monthly after-tax income. Include employer 401(k) match and any other automatic savings. This is your periodic contribution amount for the future value formula.

Use the future value of a lump sum plus annuity formula, or a simple online calculator, to project when your current balance plus monthly contributions will reach your FI number. Use 7% real return (after inflation) for conservative planning.

Test what happens if you increase contributions by $200/month, $500/month, or $1,000/month. Seeing the concrete impact of a savings rate increase — often shaving 2-5 years off your FI timeline — makes the trade-offs tangible and motivating.

For long-term stock market projections, use 7% for inflation-adjusted (real) returns or 10% for nominal returns based on the S&P 500 historical average. For a more conservative estimate, use 6% real. For bond-heavy portfolios, use 3-4% real. Always specify whether you are using nominal or real returns — mixing them up is one of the most common planning mistakes.

Future value calculations show what WOULD happen if returns were constant every year. In reality, markets fluctuate — you might earn 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Over 20-30 year periods, average returns tend to converge toward historical norms, making future value projections reasonably useful for planning. Treat them as directional estimates, not guarantees.

Future value asks: "What will $10,000 today be worth in 20 years?" Present value asks the reverse: "What is $50,000 in 20 years worth in today's dollars?" They use the same variables but in opposite directions. Present value is useful for evaluating whether a future payout (like a pension or annuity) is worth the cost today.

The Rule of 72 works for any compounding rate, including inflation. At 3% inflation, prices double every 24 years (72 / 3 = 24). This means $50,000 in annual spending today becomes $100,000 in 24 years in nominal terms — your purchasing power is halved if your income stays flat. This is why investing in assets that outpace inflation is essential.

For FI planning, future value is more intuitive — it tells you what your portfolio will grow to. However, the most practical approach is to calculate future value using real (after-inflation) returns. This effectively gives you a future value stated in today's purchasing power, which is what you actually need to know for spending planning.

In tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), your investments compound without tax drag, so the standard future value formula works directly. In taxable accounts, capital gains taxes, dividend taxes, and tax-loss harvesting all affect your real return. A rough adjustment is to reduce your assumed return by 0.5-1.0% for taxable accounts to account for ongoing tax drag.

Future value calculations are the most practical tool in the FI planner's toolkit. They turn abstract concepts like compound growth and savings rate into concrete dollar amounts and specific timelines. The key takeaways are straightforward: use 7% real returns for conservative planning, always account for inflation by using real rather than nominal returns, and remember that your monthly contribution rate has a far larger impact on the outcome than chasing an extra point or two of return. The Rule of 72 gives you instant mental math for any investment decision — how long to double, what rate you need, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. Combined with a clear FI number and a disciplined savings rate, future value projections show you exactly when financial independence becomes reality. Run the numbers, test different scenarios, and let the math motivate you to increase that monthly contribution whenever you can.

#8978. Bikepacking America's Longest Multiuse Trail Network

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Gas-station pizza, a medieval-themed hotel, canal and railroad bike path. Experience New York's multitudes on the Empire State Trail.

Even the slightest rain can sound thunderous inside a tent—and this was not slight rain. It came down in buckets, just as my partner Maggie and I were settling into our sleeping bags. I worried whether the barely-two-person tent would withstand a deluge like this and what the protocol was should lightning strike. And then lightning struck.

We talked about what to do. Maggie pulled up some information on her phone and was soon crouching on one foot, to avoid creating a circuit, she said with confidence. She counted the seconds between each flash and rumble out loud to gauge the storm’s proximity to us. I was mostly thinking of just how scant our escape options were. Our only way out was our drenched bicycles, resting against a soggy pine tree outside the tent. We took turns proposing different plans: spend the night in the campsite bathrooms, ride to the nearest motel, call the cops. We settled on hoping for the best. I fell asleep amid spiraling thoughts of dread: first night in, and this bike trip was already feeling like a mistake.

I woke up to the sound of birdsong and gentle raindrops, one beckoning me out of my sleeping bag, the other making a convincing argument to burrow deeper into it. But multiday bike touring, I would come to learn by the end of a 10-day journey across New York State’s Empire State Trail, is all about convincing yourself to do things you might not feel like doing—ride another dozen miles to the next town because it’s either that or a soulless highway motel, eat yet another granola bar because you didn’t plan lunch properly, wake up early to beat the hottest hours of the day—only to be thankful, eventually, that you did them.

Under a canopy of drizzle, Maggie and I emerged from our tent and went about a set of tasks that would soon become routine: We boiled water on our tiny camp stove for coffee and tea, broke down our sopping tent, repacked our panniers, and triple-checked that we left nothing behind. We were exhausted—a bad sign considering this was Day Two. But it was understandable, given how much we’d already experienced.

Starting in Buffalo, we’d decided to take a 65-mile pre-trip detour, cycling to Niagara Falls before looping back to start our real journey on the Empire State Trail that would take us all the way to New York City. We had already ridden through verdant farmland and industrial blight, had meandering conversations with strangers, and contended with the elements. A douchebag in a cheap sports car had almost run us off the road, but a bike shop mechanic at Campus WheelWorks in Buffalo had fixed my moody mechanical disc brakes on our way out of town and refused payment after he saw our panniers. We were the third bike tourers who had come through that week, he told us, but the first to have chosen to go west—to the falls—before heading east. He seemed to like that.

The morning after the storm, we caught our first glimpse of the Erie Canalway Trail, the western section of the Empire State Trail, which runs 360 miles from the shores of Lake Erie in Buffalo to the Hudson River in Albany. As far as we could see, we were the only people on this section. A finely ground gravel path, compacted by the rain, ran along the canal’s edge, straight and flat. A blanket of fog cloaked the waterway in an eerie silence. We stopped for a minute to take it in. Amid the quiet, I struggled to imagine the canal as the artery of industry it once had been. It was a long way yet to New York City.

On December 31, 2020, New York’s then-governor Andrew Cuomo announced the completion of the Empire State Trail, a 750-mile bike route, 75 percent of which is on car-free paths. The trail runs from Battery Park on the southern tip of Manhattan, up through the Hudson Valley and the Adirondacks to the border with Canada. Another section runs from Albany, all along the Erie Canal, to Buffalo. In all, it’s the largest multiuse trail network in the country.

While most sections existed before the establishment of the Empire State Trail, it took roughly four years—and about $200 million—to link them into a continuous network, a process that involved stakeholders ranging from individual municipalities to community volunteer groups, to the state’s parks department. “[The Empire State Trail is] easily 50 percent of my job now,” says Christopher Morris, the statewide trails program planner for New York State Parks, Recreation, and Historic Preservation. The trail isn’t overseen by a single entity; rather, it’s a kind of amorphous commonwealth of invested parties, each looking after their own section in favor of this greater mission. A major part of Morris’s job involves getting the word out, he says. He often gets emails from would-be travelers, from both the U.S. and abroad, looking for tips on how to navigate the trail. “When you really see this kind of investment make a difference, it’s rewarding,” he says. “It makes you feel good about your job.”

It’s understandable if you missed this bit of nerdy infrastructure news when the trail system opened. December 2020 was, up until that point, the deadliest month of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States. Over the preceding eight months, I’d holed away in a one-bedroom apartment in Manhattan, overwhelmed by a sense that the world I’d known and loved had ended. I’d spent the entirety of the previous year hopping week by week from destination to destination as The 52 Places Traveler for the New York Times, so the abrupt transition to total stasis left me feeling helpless—not to mention jobless. I welcomed the Empire State Trail news, which I heard about from hours of scrolling through Reddit looking for something—anything—to bring me out of my apartment and into the world again. Around four years earlier, I had splurged on a Trek CrossRip, a jack-of-all-trades, gravel-ish bike with an aluminum frame, after a lifetime of secondhand clunkers. Over time, I had made little upgrades—a Brooks saddle, handlebar tape that didn’t bleed dye onto my palms, bombproof Schwalbe tires to withstand New York City, where the streets are paved with glass. In the darkest days of the pandemic, that bike became my ticket out.

I rode whenever I could—through the empty streets of the city, the usual din of life being lived replaced by the constant wail of sirens; up and down the Hudson River Greenway on Manhattan’s West Side, itself part of the Empire State Trail. At around the same time I’d sprung for the Trek, Maggie had bought a Specialized Dolce, an aluminum all-rounder with rim brakes and what the company calls “Women’s Endurance Geometry.” She also fell in love with Brooks’s leather saddles and added in-line brake levers for extra safety. Together, we ventured farther afield. We followed the Empire State Trail up through the succession of rail trails in the Hudson Valley, veering off it to visit a friend in the Catskills. In the summer of 2021, I rented a car and drove my bike 275 miles up to Lake Champlain, where I explored the network’s most northerly sections through the Adirondacks, where the “trail” often is just a lane painted onto the side of a road—some of the 25 percent that isn’t car-free. I took locals’ advice to deviate from the main roads onto quieter country lanes, but I also found the rumble of logging trucks and tourist campervans whizzing by me oddly comforting, for it signaled a return to some kind of normalcy.

Spending so much time in transit for work has made home a moving target to me, often just out of reach and always out of focus. The bicycle, a tool invented to traverse distances efficiently, helped me see what was right in front of me.

In the early months of 2023, started to sketch out a trip I hoped would feel like a culmination of all my backyard wanderings around New York. Travel has always been a shortcut to adventure to me, and, because of that, I’ve often shorthanded adventure as requiring distance. I wondered if I could tap into the same thrills, all without ever stepping foot on a jet plane.

After a 10-hour train ride from New York City to Buffalo, I’d ride two main sections of the Empire State Trail—the west-to-east Erie Canal Trailway and the chain of rail trails and backroads running south from Albany back to my Harlem apartment—some 550 miles in all. Burdened by corporate vacation policies, Maggie decided she’d ride the Erie Canal section to Albany with me, then hop on the train home. In the months leading up to the trip, I pored over guides and online forums, of which there are many, building out a plan that involved a mix of camping and staying at bed-and-breakfasts in the towns along the way. Veterans of the trail warned of heavily trafficked sections of road around Kingston in the Hudson Valley and of the mosquitoes that swarmed the campsites at the various lock stations of the Erie Canal. Insiders cautioned against underestimating the coma-inducing qualities of a Rochester “garbage plate,” a bucketload of ground meat smothered in a fridge-tray’s worth of condiments. I took fastidious notes and drew up packing lists, weighing my panniers until I got to a weight I felt comfortable with. I plotted out days on the trail that would run us an average mileage of around 60, with a few “rest days” in the 30s baked in.

Seasoned bikepackers and bike tourers may find this all a little overdramatic. But having really only fallen hard for cycling in the last few years, I still don’t understand many things: a bike’s head-tube angle and trail; heart-rate zones and watts. But I do know travel. I know that so many of the clichés are true: that the best travel moments often appear out of the haze of the unexpected; that the journey can mean much more than the destination; that risk almost always reaps rewards; that who you travel with is often more important than where you go; that everywhere, no matter how seemingly mundane or obscure, has a little bit of magic waiting to reveal itself, if you just let it.

When it opened in 1825, the Erie Canal was the longest artificial waterway in North America and, in how it opened up the interior of the country to enterprising East Coasters, it was an embodiment of a pioneer mindset that saw a burgeoning country shape the land to its will and expand farther west. While it wouldn’t take long for the railway to replace canal barges as the go-to freight hauler, the political will and sheer toil that went into the canal’s construction would be a precursor to the hyper-capitalist nation emerging in the following centuries. “In time, this skinny ditch in upstate New York would demonstrate that trade and commerce are keys to the expansion of prosperity and freedom itself,” writes the historian Peter L. Bernstein in his 2005 history of the canal, The Wedding of the Waters.

Many of the settlements along the canal aren’t thriving like they were when this was a major thoroughfare of trade. Once tracing a path between vibrant industrial hubs, the waterway now closely mirrors the contours of the Rust Belt. Just as the grandeur of Victorian mansions points to what was, so do empty streets and faded “For Rent” signs on empty storefronts.

One such town, Brockport, is at least partially buoyed by the state university campus—or so I was told by Valerie Ciciotti, who runs Park Ave B&B in a painstakingly restored 1851 mansion that we stayed in. Graduation is the busiest time, she says, but bike tourists like us are becoming more common every summer. As we rolled out of Brockport the next morning, I wondered—not for the last time—whether a steady influx of tired, hungry cyclists could be enough to keep towns along the canal alive. (When I caught up with Ciciotti recently, she said the trail was already making a difference—the village government has become more directly involved with tourism, including designating Brockport an official Empire State Trail Town.)

We spent the next week on the Erie Canal in a kind of meditative rhythm that only comes from long trips, drifting in and out of conversations with each other, keeping count of kingfishers flitting along the water, and gasping when a heron swallowed a fish whole.

Outside Fairport, the skies turned black and dumped rain on us until we were laughing at the absurdity of trying to cycle through mud so dense it made our tires seize. Bystanders, wise enough to take shelter, cheered us on as we rode. We stopped under an awning and pried mud from our chains with our fingers. When the rain showed no sign of stopping, we just kept going—pulled along by the promise of a hot shower and a cold beer. We rode through sheets of rain until water poured out of our shoes. Once the deluge slowed, we tied wet clothes to our bikes. We looked like sailboats rolling down the trail.

One night, we camped at one of the locks along the trail, where boats are lifted to account for elevation changes in the ground. (Cyclists can camp at certain locks for free but are encouraged to call the lockkeeper ahead of time as a courtesy.) As the light faded and the mosquitoes emerged, I spoke to a pair of retirees on a boat who were following the same path as so many goods-bearing barges once did—from the Great Lakes to the Hudson and the sea. We woke up in the middle of the night to the infernal shrieks of nearby foxes. The following morning, we rode into Utica for breakfast at Golden’s diner, itself a throwback, where one man behind a counter flipped eggs and pointed to the self-service coffee station while bebop played from tinny speakers.

For our last night on the canal, we stayed in the Amsterdam Castle, which looms over the tiny town of Amsterdam like a tyrant’s keep. A bizarre manifestation of some sort of Arthurian fantasy, the hotel features suits of armor in the lobby and velvet bedding in the rooms. New York State truly contains multitudes.

I thought about all the many things I’d seen and done in my travels to far-flung places—witnessing a solar eclipse in Chile, kayaking alongside humpbacks in Antarctica, hiking through prehistoric rainforests in New Zealand. If novelty is what drives our travel decisions, it was rapidly becoming clear to me that I didn’t always need to fling myself halfway around the world to find it.

Because the Empire State Trail is mostly a consolidation of existing paths and an effort to fill the gaps between them—and because of the vast distances the network covers—the character of the trail changes the farther along it you ride. I noticed this as soon as I said goodbye to Maggie in Albany at the eastern terminus of the Erie Canal and turned south on the first of a number of rail trails that would take me back to New York City over the next three days. With the canal no longer a constant companion, I found myself instead passing through bucolic suburbs, open farmland, and, occasionally, dense sections of forest. Riding alone after days with someone else was an adjustment, too. I found, just a few hours after turning south, I was talking to myself—making observations about the lack of shade and the odd, ashy taste in my mouth from forest fire smoke drifting south from Canada. It made for tough riding—and I took much more frequent rest stops.

When planning my trip, I knew I’d pass through major regional hubs like Hudson and Kingston. But I also wanted to experience corners of the state I hadn’t seen before, and I chose my stops for the night with that in mind. That’s how I ended up veering a mile off the trail into the storybook village of Kinderhook. I checked into the luxurious Old Dutch Inn, a new hotel housed in a modernized 19th-century building with views of the village square. It had only just opened a few weeks prior. The co-owner, Jennifer Ose-MacDonald, showed no trepidation when she welcomed my mud-streaked, sweat-drenched self into her immaculate establishment, where snow-white linens hung from the windows. Knowing I was one of the first of what she hoped to be many bike-traveler guests, she asked me for advice on bike racks. I told her that though the exact model of bike rack wasn’t that important, alas, a lot of cyclists might not be as comfortable locking up their bikes outside overnight as I was. (Ose-MacDonald says she has since carved out space for indoor bike storage and has added a trove of tools for cycling guests.)

Ose-Macdonald’s partner, Jake Samascott, runs a much-visited orchard and farm shop in town but is also the president of the Columbia Friends of the Electric Trail, an organization of volunteers who maintain the section of trail that passes through Columbia County, mowing and trimming the greenery around the path. For years it was an unused, overgrown corridor through which power lines ran. More than a thoroughfare for bike tourists like me, the trail is a community asset, Samascott says. “I have three little girls who wanted to learn to ride bikes—I want them riding on a trail and not on the road.”

I saw how these paths build community throughout my trip but especially on the rail trails that run one into another through the Hudson Valley until they end in Van Cortlandt Park in the Bronx. Travelers like me were few and far between, but I passed dozens of families out on bikes, joggers with their dogs, even summer-school groups. Several, seeing my bags, and the level of grime on my face and body, would offer a thumbs-up or shout, “You’re almost there,” though they didn’t know where I was going.

New York State isn’t all smooth-rolling. Idyllic sections of tree-shaded gravel paths on rail trails are broken up by hilly roads and, at one point around Kingston, a traffic-snarled bridge. Unlike the Erie Canal section, campsites along the Albany-NYC axis of the trail are largely nonexistent, which means budgeting for hotels, and that can be pricey, especially during the summer high season. The penultimate stretch of trail, leading to the town of Brewster, inches steadily uphill for at least 15 miles, which, after more than a week of long days, felt like I was conquering the Dolomites. Arriving in Brewster—still about 50 miles from the northern edge of New York City—I found none of the charming, independent B&Bs or idyllic campsites I had depended so much on during my trip. I could have opted to make a break for it and ride a century straight from the Poughkeepsie area to the city on my last day, but I didn’t have it in me. I bought a gas-station beer the size of my head, checked into a soulless Comfort Inn, and ordered a pizza.

Over the course of the whole trip, 11 days in all, I thought often about infrastructure and movement; about how much effort has gone into inventing new ways to travel, ever faster, ever cheaper, ever more efficient. By the time the Erie Canal was completed, the railroad was already ascendant. On large sections of the Hudson Valley’s various rail trails, the rusted remains of iron rails sit, fossilized and inert. Alongside them, on the very beds of dirt where they once ran, the gravel is crisscrossed with bike-tire tracks and packed down with the footprints of millions of pedestrians.

I stopped often, to stretch, to photograph, to think. As it does when traveling on your own power, every mile felt like an achievement, no matter how repetitive and, at moments, no matter how difficult the actions were. Even while choking on smoke, with my legs burning and my bike making new and unfamiliar sounds (brake rub, it turned out), I found myself drawn onward by a sense of discovery—the feeling that I was getting a more solid picture of a concept that has eluded me for most of my life: home.

The closer I got to New York City, the more anything resembling silence was replaced with the constant whir of nearby interstates. Planes rumbled overhead. How much faster can we possibly go? What comes next in our constant hunt for peak efficiency? And what will we do with all that extra free time, anyway? The bike and all the places it can take me beckon.

Sebastian Modak is a writer, editor, and photographer based in New York City. He spent 2019 circling the globe as the New York Times 52 Places Traveler, reporting from every destination on the Times’ 52 Places to Go list.

#8976. VO2 Max by Age: All You Need to Know About This Performance Metric

A strong case for continuing to ride as you get older.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Most cyclists, at some point, want to see how fast and hard they can go, even for just a few minutes. Riding at that nearly all-out intensity, when you’re breathing heavy and can barely talk, is likely your VO₂ max (or close to it). Scientifically speaking, VO2 max is the maximum amount of oxygen your body can take in and use and it’s a marker of your cardiovascular fitness level.

For a variety of reasons, VO₂ max naturally decreases as you get older. Fortunately, athletes are more likely to minimize this decline through consistent and purposeful training.

Read on for more information about VO₂ max by age, including how it’s determined, and how to make sure your rides help maintain this important metric as you get older.

Of all the available health and fitness metrics, VO₂ max is one of the most important. “VO₂ max is the amount of oxygen that you can breathe in, transport to the muscle, and utilize during maximal exertion and aerobic exercise,” Todd Buckingham, Ph.D., exercise physiologist at PTSportsPRO in Grand Rapids, Michigan tells Bicycling.

He explains that, besides being an indicator of overall fitness, it’s also a “gold standard” measurement of an athlete’s ability to perform well in an endurance event; essentially, the higher your VO₂ max, the greater your potential. “Once your VO₂ max gets to a certain level, other things like lactate threshold and exercise efficiency come into play. But VO₂ max is the first step in determining performance,” Buckingham says.

VO₂ max, which is measured as milliliters of oxygen per kilogram of bodyweight per minute (ml/kg/min), is most accurately assessed in a laboratory environment. During the test, you wear a specialized mask that measures inhaled oxygen and exhaled carbon dioxide while you pedal an exercise bike, run on a treadmill, or swim in a pool. Over the course of 12 to 15 minutes, you increase the exercise intensity so that, by the end of the test, you pushed your aerobic limits.

Getting access to a lab can obviously be time consuming and expensive, so you can also turn to your fitness tracker to help establish a baseline and keep tabs on how your fitness is improving. The caveat: You have to take those numbers with a grain of salt. Research shows that many wearables over- or underestimate VO₂ max by up to 10 percent.

Like many markers of health and fitness, VO₂ max naturally declines as you age. “VO₂ max tends to peak for men in their mid-to-late 20s. For women, it’s a little later, like early 30s. But after it reaches the peak, it tends to decrease,” Buckingham says.

Some research indicates that the average person can expect around a 10 percent decline in VO₂ max after age of 30. (This is particularly true for males, the study suggests.) However, the drop may be even more drastic among athletes. According to a study published in a 2024 issue of Experimental Gerontology, aging had a greater affect on VO₂ max in female runners than in sedentary women. The scientists hypothesized that the younger athletes started with a higher VO₂ max than their sedentary peers and, therefore, had further to fall. Despite this more drastic decline, active women still had better VO2 max than their non-active peers.

Generally speaking, though, age-related reductions in VO₂ max are likely due to a combination of factors, including a reduction in cardiac output. Cardiac ouput is the product of the number of times your heart beats per minute (heart rate) and the volume of blood ejected with each contraction of the heart (stroke volume). As you age, both the amount of blood your heart pumps out to the body and your maximal heart rate go down. Older individuals may also experience a reduction in blood circulation.

Age-related muscle loss, a.k.a. sarcopenia, may also be to blame for a decline in VO₂ max. “We tend to lose muscle mass and increase body fat percentage [as we get older],” Buckingham says. “Because fat does not have mitochondria and capillaries to turn oxygen into energy, we have metabolically inactive tissue.” (Mitochondria are the parts of cells that use oxygen to manufacture adenosine triphosphate (ATP), our primary energy currency.)

In other words, with lower muscle mass comes the loss of capillaries and mitochondria, making your body less energy efficient.

Wondering what’s a typical rate of decline for VO₂ max? The chart below contains research-based averages of VO₂ max by age and fitness level, for men and women. Remember that each individual’s VO₂ max score depends on multiple biological and lifestyle factors; these are just a range of average scores.

While everyone gets older, not everyone loses VO₂ max at the same rate. “There’s the saying, ‘We don’t stop exercising because we get old. We get old because we stop exercising,’” Buckingham says. “Just by being active, you can prolong that level of VO₂ max. Obviously, at some point, the atrophy process is going to occur. It just happens as we get older. But you can maintain it for a lot longer when you’re active than if you were just sedentary.”

If you’re already following a training program that includes a mix of easy, steady-state rides, more intense workouts, and strength training, stick with that diversified approach.

Lower intensity, or “zone 2” workouts are especially important. “When you are exercising at lower intensities, you produce more mitochondria and capillaries. Mitochondria is where the oxygen is transformed into energy, and the capillaries are the vessels that actually take the oxygen from the blood to get it into the muscle to then get it into the mitochondria to produce energy,” Buckingham explains.

Higher-intensity exercise is also essential, as it increases the size of each mitochondrion (“so we can get more oxygen into it,” Buckingham says). High-intensity exercise, Buckingham explains, necessitates a longer recovery period.

To maximize the benefits of your workouts while avoiding burnout, Buckingham recommends the 80/20 training methodology: 80 percent of your workouts are low-intensity and 20 percent are performed at higher intensities.

Strength training is also critical, as it can combat sarcopenia and maintain muscle mass. As previously noted, muscle mass is critical to VO₂ max, as it contains mitochondria and capillaries.

A pretty valid case for making these workouts a part of your regular routine: Research suggests that higher VO₂ max levels may be associated with a longer lifespan. One study published by the Journal of the American College of Cardiology followed a cohort of more than 5,000 men for 46 years. Researchers found that higher rates of cardiorespiratory fitness, as determined by VO₂ max, were associated with longer lives.

#8975. Triathlon News, October 2026: Ironman Crashes, NYC Tri Returns, Middle East Racing

Tim Heming highlights the biggest news in triathlon in October 2026. (Photo: Triathlete)

In October, the triathlon world turned its eyes to the Big Island for another epic edition of the Ironman World Championship, but that didn’t stop the rest of the multisport world from serving up its usual mix of drama, debate, and headline-grabbing news.

From analyzing the sparse participation numbers at New York’s long-awaited race return to tackling safety, transparency, and course caps following a scary collision on the Queen K, October delivered plenty of food for thought. And, as always, contributor Tim Heming is here to digest it with you.

The first line of Sarah Wassner Flynn’s article about the return of the iconic New York City Triathlon, published earlier this year, reads: “For more than two decades, the New York City Triathlon was one of the sport’s most iconic races. Debuting in 2001, it quickly became a bucket-list event for age-groupers and pros alike.”

The piece previewed this year’s race return, renamed the Big Apple Triathlon, under new ownership of Alpha Win, formerly known as HITS Endurance, with Tommy Struzzieri taking over the company from his father, Tom.

Alpha Win, based in Saugerties, New York, is no novice when it comes to race hosting. They have put on over 200 races, but making a success of this one offered the sternest test of their credentials to date.

Held on October 10, the day when most eyes in the triathlon world were focused almost 5,000 miles west on the Big Island of Hawaii, would it prove enough of a draw to justify the set-up costs of a swim in the Hudson River, a bike up the closed West Side Highway, and a run through Central Park?

Since its halcyon days, the event has been beset by problems, with participation tumbling from a peak of almost 4,000 during its time as part of the Life Time Fitness Series in 2010. In 2024, it was canceled by new owner Supertri before registration even opened, with organizers saying they couldn’t find a suitable date. It didn’t return in 2025 either, which, given Supertri’s focus on producing stylish, short-course events in major urban areas, had to be a worrying sign.

“We’re just trying to bring back something that athletes have been asking for,” Struzzieri said in March, noting that numbers would be capped at 2,500. If that felt optimistic, a New York Post piece on the eve of the event recounted its troubled history and asked: Is this time the charm? stating that around 1,300 athletes were expected to start, with prices ranging from $350–$650.

The results, however, show fewer than half that number: only around 600 finishers across all formats, the lowest the event has seen since it began in 2001. “Every year that there’s an issue with this event, it hurts the event the following year,” Scott Nilson, Supertri’s U.S. general manager of events, told us in 2024. Perhaps this year it will be the simple economics of numbers.

Registration for the 2027 event is now open with early-bird pricing (including processing fees) at $548.90 (Olympic distance) and $383.90 (sprint distance). Triathlete reached out to Alpha Win for comment.

For the majority, the Ironman World Championship is a day of celebration and achievement. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience, the ultimate triathlon dream. For Trish Byron, that dream turned into a nightmare.

Byron was struck by a male cyclist from behind almost 30 miles into the bike leg, leaving her with seven fractured ribs, a broken collarbone, a punctured and partially collapsed lung, a concussion, a laceration requiring stitches, and extensive road rash.

It’s understood the cyclist stopped and spoke with volunteers before continuing the race, but Byron’s daughter Cassie Anne put out a plea on Facebook for more information, saying: “We’re hoping to gather firsthand accounts, identify the cyclist involved, and better understand what happened.”

Accidents happen, but the incident raises questions about transparency when serious collisions occur during races. Should such incidents be publicly reported, both to demonstrate that appropriate safety protocols and follow-up procedures have been followed and to help triathletes better understand the risks involved in signing up?

Cassie Anne’s post received a response from Judy Daggett, who said: “This exact scenario happened to me on the bike about mile 85, causing me to crash also. The guy who hit me kept going. Another athlete helped me to my feet.

“I immediately had double vision and said, ‘Yes, I need help,’ but there was no one around. I managed to get back on the bike and ride to T2, praying my vision didn’t completely leave.

“When I got there, they took me by ambulance to the ER for a CT of my head, thinking I could possibly have a brain bleed. Thankfully, I did not, but I also have fractured ribs, a hip and shoulder injury, and a concussion.”

Daggett went on to say she’d reached out to Ironman but was yet to hear from them, stating it was her first DNF in 30 years and that the “men were so aggressive, they need to let them go first”.

Her final point relates to the questions raised about the scheduled swim start waves that interspersed the men’s and women’s age-group divisions in Hawaii, whereas previously, the men had been started earlier in one cohort, followed by the women.

It also brings into focus the broader question (that has continued to surface since the announcement of the return to one day of racing) of whether Ironman should cap numbers on the course for both fairness and safety reasons.

While it might seem that Trish Byron’s family shouldn’t have far to go to find answers, as Anna Grosz, who also responded to the post, explained, it might not be that simple: “I provided medical support for the race. We are bound by patient confidentiality laws. You should reach out to Ironman through official channels. The medical director may be able to communicate directly with the affected athlete, but course volunteers cannot do so.”

Triathlete has contacted Ironman for comment.

Championship season is not quite over in the world of triathlon. The T100 Tour still has three events on the calendar, with Dubai and Saudi Arabia in November ahead of the T100 World Championship Final in Qatar. The action in the Middle East will also continue with the 2026 World Triathlon Multisport Championship in Abu Dhabi.

The headlines will be the professional races over 100K where Hayden Wilde looks to be the odds-on favorite to retain his title, and it’s wide open on the women’s side. But there is also shorter-distance racing and representative age-group competition throughout.

Despite conflict in the region and the cancelation, postponement or relocation of other major sporting events, particularly in Saudi Arabia, both World Triathlon and the Professional Triathletes Organization are, for now, proceeding as planned. That’s perhaps to be expected, with contingency decisions often left until the last possible moment. But if the events do go ahead, it will be interesting to see how much appetite international athletes have for traveling to the region.

Conversations around weight can be a sensitive topic: triggering to some, frustrating to others, and almost irrelevant to others. And Susan Kitchen’s article on why we shouldn’t be concerning ourselves with post-race weight gain will no doubt grab the attention of athletes who might have concerns about how they can be heavier after doing all that exercise.

While Kitchen spells out the reasons here (which, spoiler alert, can be perfectly natural as your body recovers), it also made me think that perhaps the concern shouldn’t be how much you weigh, but why, in the days following an incredible endurance feat, you’re not off celebrating somewhere, rather than hopping on the scale.

You may not find an answer as to which is better, but there is plenty we can learn from Jordan Blanco’s roundtable discussion with triathlon legends Flora Duffy and Jan Frodeno when it comes to their appreciation for the pinnacle events in our sport – including that the 2008 win in Beijing was Frodeno’s first-ever elite victory!

But if there is one takeaway, then it’s probably that following your heart is the first step, and the financial rewards will follow. Doing it the other way around might just be a little tougher.

What do we learn from the Kona bike mechanics recounting tales from the Big Island?

Number one: That most of us should probably invest a bit more time in understanding how to fix our own bikes.

Number two: That whatever daft mistake you’ve made, it won’t be the dumbest thing they’ve seen (one athlete rolled up with two front wheels and no back, another with two back wheels and no front).

Number three: If you do have a problem, get to the mechanics early (the day before race day was the busiest).

And number four: Have a little patience. “That’s really the hardest part of Ironman week – managing athletes’ timeline expectations,” Taylor Bushong, a traveling race mechanic working out of Bike Works Kona, told Sara Stover. “Managing the unrealistic ‘can you just’ requests. The understanding of the level of the request seems to be outside the scope of recognition.”

But while being a bike mechanic sounds like a thankless task, it has some upsides. The real kicker, featuring five carbon wheels and the town’s dump, is cleverly left until the final line.

Some charitable sporting endeavors fall flat while others just fly, and often there seems to be no logic as to which cause will capture the public mood.

Thankfully, for Ethan Hunger, the idea to complete a world-record number of super sprint triathlons within 24 hours to raise money for his local food bank in Bellingham, Washington, really took off.

If ever there was a classic case of nominative determinism, then this is it. Hunger v. Hunger actually started following the COVID pandemic, but as Travis Mundell found out, this year’s challenge was the most ambitious yet, helping push the initiative’s total fundraising beyond $1.2 million.

It’s life-affirming to see such dedication in action, not just from Hunger, but from the community that rolled out to support him, where putting all the proper procedures in place so the record could be ratified by Guinness reads as more grueling than all that swimming, biking, and running.

There’s probably not much more that needs adding to one of the most dramatic Ironman World Championship races in living memory. Having written a reaction piece on how the house (in this case, the Big Island) always wins versus the gambler, I’ve reflected more on how it just seems such a difficult race to get right. My first thought: If the pros can’t do it (see the DNF files here), what chance do the mere mortals have? Follow-up thought: Nobody racing here could ever be described as a mere mortal anyway.

#8974. Can’t get back into working out? It’s not a motivation problem.

Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?

Hundreds of you wrote back. Thoughtful, honest answers. Thank you.

And one theme jumped out at me IMMEDIATELY.

One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, said it this way:

If you’ve ever had a great run (for a few days or a few years) and then couldn’t find your way back, this one’s for you, too.

I’ve heard this so many times in my coaching career. You were in a really good groove. Something knocked you off. And getting back on track feels incredibly difficult, and you don’t know why.

I’ve experienced this myself! I was in a groove with food logging. It felt easy. Then I took a break, and when I tried to start up again, I couldn’t get it going with any consistency for the life of me.

Here’s my take after nearly two decades of coaching: I doubt this is a motivation thing.

You were cruising at 70 miles an hour. You made a pit stop, and now you’re trying to jump the car straight back to 70. Instantly.

Another reader put it really well in their message to me:

That’s driving with your eyes on the rearview mirror. And it makes anything smaller feel like it doesn’t count.

But smaller is how you get back up to speed.

After multiple false starts with food logging, I realized I was falling into the same trap. And instead of forcing myself to weigh and measure anything, I gave myself a different on-ramp. Protein and veggies at each meal? Check. That allowed me to build back up again and find the groove that worked for me in this current phase of life.

Previous success can feel like a scorecard that you have to grade yourself against.

But what worked before might not work for you right now.

And it’s important to remember that most of us needed an on-ramp the first time, too. That part didn’t change after some time off.

You know what you “should” be doing. Let’s put that aside for now.

Instead, let’s shrink down what our focus is. We don’t have to figure out the whole routine. Not the whole week. Let’s work on today.

Try this thought experiment with me: if you didn’t have any expectations of what this “should” look like, what is one thing that feels doable today?

Maybe it’s performing your warm-up routine. Or doing the first round of exercises in your workout.

Maybe it’s batch cooking some protein tonight, or running to the grocery store to stock up on some easy fruit and veggie options.

Try it out, and see how that feels. Is the resistance still there? If it isn’t, you’ve found the start of your on-ramp. 🙌

And if it still feels hard to start? That’s OK, too. We can choose a different entry point and try again.

If you’re in that camp of “I know what to do. I can’t get myself to start,” give yourself a different, smaller on-ramp.

But it may be exactly what you need right now.

Hit reply and let me know what yours looks like.

#8973. A WorldTour Rider Shared His Tire Pressure. It’s Lower Than You Think.

His answer was striking even in an era when road tire pressures keep dropping.

An Instagram Reel featuring world tour pro Luke Plapp (Team Jayco-AlUla) talking about tire pressure appeared in my Instagram feed and caught my attention, mostly because many pro riders either won't tell you or don’t know their tire pressure, and most team mechanics won’t openly share that information with the press. Now, I’ve been on the lower-is-generally-better tire-pressure train for many years. I routinely run my road bike tires between 50 and 70 psi, depending on the bike, tire, and wheel setup. I was still struck by how low Plapp’s number was, even by modern standards.

The clip comes from the September 23, 2026, episode of Stanley St. Social podcast. Plapp says he gets the same reaction whenever he tells people what pressure he runs. “This is actually one where every single time I tell people what tire pressure I run, every punter all over the world just can't believe it, so we're running 32mm tires at 3.7 to 3.8 bar.” That works out to 53.7 to 55.1 psi.

Plapp calls them 32mm tires. But the team is using CADEX Aero 30mm, so his quote likely refers to their mounted width. I haven’t measured the exact setup of the CADEX Ultra 50 wheels, which use a hookless rim with a 22.4mm internal width and 30mm external width with the CADEX Aero 30mm tire. But I’ve ridden these particular tires and reviewed the CADEX 50 Ultra for Bicycling. In my test, a nominal 28mm CADEX Race tire measured close to 30mm on the 22.4mm internal rim. So it’s very reasonable to assume that a labeled 30mm tire would inflate closer to 32mm. You can read my CADEX 50 Ultra wheelset review here.

The biggest piece of information that we don’t have from this clip is Plapp’s actual weight. His Pro Cycling Stats page lists him as 158.75 lbs, which may or may not be accurate. But using that as an estimate puts Plapp firmly on the lower end of the tire-pressure spectrum, as I would expect someone that weight to run closer to the low-sixties psi based on various tire pressure calculators. That means Plapp is either a bit lighter than PCS thinks he is, or he simply prefers the added comfort and grip of running lower pressure.

But why is any of this interesting? For one, I generally agree with Plapp’s inferred assessment that many riders still run too much tire pressure. That’s generally been true when I talk to folks in my riding circles. Because of this, I think many riders simply don’t understand just how low performance-oriented riders have gone with their tire pressure. So if you don’t want to hear it from me, I hope hearing it from Plapp, who has raced the Tour de France for the last two years, will be more convincing.

Finally, the brief quote also highlights that if you care about your performance and optimize your tire pressure, you shouldn't take the labeled tire size at face value. Instead, you need to actually measure your tires inflated on the wheelset you are using. Just because something is labeled as 30mm doesn't mean it will measure 30mm on your wheels, and that can change the tire-pressure math in a meaningful way.

If you don’t know where to start with tire pressure, read this story, then check out my recommended tire-pressure calculators to dial in your setup.

#8972. New Pedals, No Problem: How to Install Pedals Without Damaging Your Bike

Avoid stripped crank threads and costly repairs with this step-by-step pedal swap guide.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

There are few part swaps I have seen cause more damage on a bike than an incorrectly installed set of pedals. I’ve seen experienced and beginner cyclists make a pedal installation mistake causing damage to both the pedal and the crank—resulting in anywhere from a little under $100 of damage to over $500. In some cases threads can be cleaned up and parts can be saved, but too many times this small part install can lead to hundreds of dollars in repairs.

Two of the most common ways I have seen this mistake happen are from a pedal going in at an angle into the threads of the crank or the pedals being installed on the wrong side of the cranks. If the system is damaged beyond repair, then parts need to be replaced.

Another way this can go wrong is if the pedals are not fully torqued during the installation to the cranks. When I ran a shop I’ve had customers come in that tried to install pedals at home, but the pedals backed out mid ride. When this happens it can be both a safety issue for the rider and cause damage to the bike. The good news is when done right this is a straightforward install process that can be done at home. The right tools, an easy-to-follow guide, and some attention are all you need to avoid some of the most common pedal installation issues. Below we have your guide on everything you need to know about installing your new pedals.

One thing to note on this method—I always begin the removal process and the final torquing of the pedals with the bike on the ground. This is because the torque that goes into the removal of the pedals and to meet the final torque specifications can cause stress on the frame and seatpost if the bike is clamped in a stand—especially for carbon posts and frames. When removing the pedals, put the bike in the stand after they don’t require force to loosen. Conversely, take the bike out of the stand during install after the pedals are properly screwed into the cranks, but before they get their final needed torque.

Pedal Wrenchor 5 or 6 mm Hex Wrench/Allen KeysBicycle Grease

To reduce the chance of damaging your bike, Bicycling always recommends consulting the manufacturer’s recommended torque setting and using a torque wrench when installing or servicing bike parts.

#8971. The New Colnago G5-X Isn’t a Bargain Gravel Bike. It’s a Fast, Refined Race Bike With Serious Italian Mystique

Riding it in Tuscany, we found a faster, more capable gravel bike that still feels like a Colnago.

The artistry of Italian masters surrounds you as you walk through the Uffizi Gallery. Botticelli, Caravaggio, Da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael. Hundreds of priceless paintings and sculptures fill the world-renowned museum’s halls and passageways. Artwork you have undoubtedly seen in books and magazines, on television, and in films lies around every corner.

But I wasn’t in Florence to study Renaissance and Baroque paintings; I visited the Uffizi only to burn off some jet lag before four days of riding in Tuscany. The next day I headed south to the region’s legendary strade bianche gravel roads to sample a new bike from one of cycling’s great Italian masters.

Many words have been written about Colnago and the brand’s history over the last few decades. For those new to bikes, Colnago is among cycling’s most storied marques and produces some of the world’s most sought-after bicycles.

The 72-year-old Italian company built much of its prestige and aura on its dedication to racing; numerous road cycling icons have raced on the brand’s steel, titanium, and carbon bikes. Colnago-made frames have won seemingly every Grand Tour, Monument, and spring classic event over the last six decades. And Colnago’s palmarès has only grown in the last decade.

The brand’s recent success and visibility have been inextricably tied to Tadej Pogačar’s dominant race-day performances. The Slovenian star has won two World Championships, five Tour de France titles, one Giro d’Italia victory, and several classics on Colnago bikes. Simply put, he is the most dominant road racer of his generation.

Yet, while Colnago is known to virtually every road racing fan and road bike aficionado, the brand isn’t usually the first to spring to mind when riders think of gravel bikes. Some of this can be chalked up to the discipline’s American roots; big U.S. brands like Specialized and Trek often dominate the bicycles, athletes, and events on the west side of the Atlantic. Even smaller American brands, such as Salsa and Enve, often come up in discussion before legacy road brands like Colnago.

A big part of this perception is Colnago’s relatively late entry into the gravel world. Like many European peers, Colnago was fashionably late to the gravel party, launching the G3-X in November 2019. Some American brands had a five-plus-year head start: Specialized’s Diverge and the GT Grade in 2014 and Salsa’s Warbird in 2012 were among the first purpose-built gravel models to hit shop floors.

That first Colnago gravel bike was based on the brand’s successful Prestige cyclocross platform (Wout van Aert won a CX World Championship on a Colnago in 2016). Compared with contemporary gravel bikes—and even some of the era—the G3-X handled quicker, with a taller bottom bracket and a shorter wheelbase. It also only featured 42mm tire clearance; while that sounds narrow in 2026, it was in the ballpark for a gravel bike seven years ago. Lauren De Crescenzo won the 2021 Unbound 200 on the G3-X.

In early 2024, Colnago followed up its initial gravel bike with two new gravel models. First up was the premium, Italian-made C68 Gravel; the G4-X followed a few months later. While both were excellent bikes, they fell more toward the all-road spectrum than gravel—as our review described: “the G4-X felt more like an aggressive all-road bike than a traditional gravel bike.” The G4-X and C68 Gravel geometry still closely matched the G3-X and had a stiff, responsive ride feel similar to Colnago’s road platforms. The bikes also lacked the tire clearance, frame mounts, and internal storage found on many top-end gravel models.

After launching the G4-X, Colnago listened to rider and racer feedback and quickly began work on a new gravel platform. The result, the all-new G5-X, is a bike designed from the ground up for modern gravel racing that distinctly rides like a Colnago. The brand’s R&D team—led by Davide Fumagalli, who podiumed in his age group at the 2022 UCI Gravel World Championships—focused on four key improvements for the brand’s third-generation gravel bike: Tire clearance, geometry, storage, and ride comfort.

I spent two of my four days in Tuscany riding the G5-X with Colnago’s product team on a blend of classic strade bianche white gravel roads, doubletrack, and technical singletrack (where a full suspension mountain bike wouldn’t be out of place). While not a full, long-term evaluation of the G5-X, it was a sampler plate of the bike’s potential.

Gravel tire widths seem to grow wider every season to improve traction, comfort, and speed in demanding terrain. Colnago increased the G5-X’s official clearance to 53mm nominal width, 8mm more than its predecessor. It now sits—along with bikes like Specialized’s Crux 5 (55mm clearance)—at a midpoint between wide and narrow tire clearance.

While certainly an improvement over earlier Colnago gravel bikes, the G5-X’s increased clearance doesn’t quite put it in the category of 57mm-clearance bikes like Canyon’s new Grail, Factor Elana, Argon 18 Dark Matter, 3T Extrema Italia, Allied Able, or Ari Shafer. On the flip side, the G5-X offers slightly more room for rubber than the Enve Mog and Trek Checkpoint (both at 50mm), and a bit more space for the rear tire than the Cervélo’s Aspero 5 (45mm rear, 51mm front) or the Cannondale Super-X (48mm rear, 51mm front).

The G5-X’s I sampled were fitted with 50mm-wide, Goodyear XPLR Inter tubeless tires. Optimized for the Zipp 303 XPLR SW wheels (also on the bikes), the Inters worked well and rolled fast on the smoother gravel roads. Their compound feels a little firm, but they have sufficient tread for braking and knobs for cornering.

However, I found the Inters lacked grip when the going got chunky, and I tore a sidewall on one while descending. These are the conditions where a wider, mountain bike-style tire would have been more appropriate. A 29”x2.1” tire (depending on the rim) would press Colnago’s 53mm max width. Perhaps a 29”x2.0” Continental Dubnital would have fit the conditions?

Colnago notes that its 53mm clearance is with the ISO-mandated 6mm clearance. So, depending on course conditions and rim width, you might be able to run slightly wider rubber on the G5-X on some days. But that also highly depends on your comfort with potentially sawing through the stays of a pricey Colnago frame.

Colnago also updated its gravel geometry to improve control over rough terrain and at higher speeds. The brand targeted three main points: A slacker head angle, a lower bottom bracket, and a longer wheelbase.

The G5-X’s slacker head angle (0.5 to 1.0 degrees on most sizes) gives riders more confidence on steeper terrain and at higher speeds. To balance the slacker HT, Colnago’s engineers also increased fork rake (by about 5mm). This maintains quick steering and avoids the vague feel of some slack bikes.

Along with the slacker head angle, Colnago increased the frame’s bottom bracket drop by 10mm, and that’s a big deal. A common trait of mountain bike geometry, it provides stability over rough terrain and a planted feeling in turns by lowering the rider’s center of mass relative to the axles. The increased drop also helps offset the taller height from wider tires and keeps the BB height from rising.

Colnago also lengthened the platform’s wheelbase. As with the head angle and bottom bracket height, this improves stability and control. The bike’s chainstays grew by 5mm across all sizes (to 435mm) while the front-center and reach measurements also increased.

On paper, this all sounds good; in the real world—especially on singletrack—the geometry proved to be brilliant. The G5-X is super composed and planted when descending and over choppy gravel road sections. The bike feels precise and refined—pick your line and take it.

Integrated storage for tools and flat-repair necessities is a must-have for many gravel riders. Sure, you can carry your pump, tube, and multitool in your jersey pocket or a seat bag, but then they rattle around or get dropped on rough roads. In-frame storage keeps those items tucked safely inside your downtube, and the weight is located low on the frame instead of swaying around on your back.

In my experience, the storage access doors on gravel and mountain bikes can be hit or miss. They all generally work, but some are overly complicated (like the scissor-design on the Cervélo Caledonia) or need to be positioned exactly right to stay in place (like the Fidlock one on the State Carbon All-Road). Finicky designs only cause frustration when trying to fix a mid-ride flat—or worse, when losing time in a race.

Colnago’s system is well thought out, feels robust, and works with a simple lever turn. The brand includes a neoprene baggy big enough to include a tube, two CO2 canisters, and a multitool.

In addition to the integrated downtube storage, the G5-X has mounts on the top tube for a bento box/feedbag and on the fork blades. However, unlike some adventure-minded gravel bikes, it has no attachment points underneath the top tube for bags, nor mounts on the rear triangle.

This seems like a missed opportunity by Colnago. While pure-racers may not need them, many riders use their gravel race bikes for overnight and light-duty bikepacking trips. Adding hidden mounts under the TT barely adds weight and looks stealthy. Plus, who wants to wrap Velcro straps around their Colnago and ruin the gorgeous aesthetic?

In our reviews of G4-X and C68 Gravel, our editors criticized the bikes’ firm ride. They rode like road race bikes, not plush, forgiving gravel grinders. The G5-X’s carbon layup and frame shaping prioritize comfort and compliance ahead of all-out sprinting stiffness.

Additionally, instead of the D-shaped post on previous gravel models, Colnago’s product team opted for a standard 27.2mm diameter round seatpost. This gives riders tons of options to tune seatpost offset, use a dropper, or choose a post with more inherent flex than Colnago’s stock carbon pillar. Like the post, other frame details make the G5-X easy to service and find replacement parts. It uses a 68mm BSA bottom bracket, a 1-⅛-inch stem, and standard-size headset bearings.

While I didn’t test any of Colnago’s previous gravel models, I do not doubt my colleagues’ impressions that those platforms were overly stiff. And while I typically like spry, racey bikes, my 50-year-old body doesn’t always agree after several hours in the saddle.

In my limited time on the G5-X, I never felt it was too stiff or overly harsh. Conversely, it did not feel muted or dull. Colnago is regarded as a master of refined ride quality, and the G5-X feels like the brand’s product team put a lot of time and effort into achieving the right balance for this new model. However, I need more ride time on the G5-X on home roads and trails to confirm if Colnago indeed ticked this box.

Colnago’s G5-X complete bike offerings are refreshingly straightforward. Two colors, three groupsets, and five frame sizes. The G5-X is (currently) not on Colnago’s customizer program or available as a frameset option.

The G5-X comes in two colors, green and blue. Both are beautiful, though perhaps not as wild as some of Colnago’s road offerings. But the bike is brand new, so we can hope to see more color variants in the future.

Colnago isn’t exactly known for producing low-cost bikes, and the G5-X certainly isn’t a budget gravel bike. However, it’s also not as eye-wateringly pricey as some of the brand’s road offerings. Colnago offers three SRAM component builds—Red XPLR AXS, Force XPLR AXS, and Rival XPLR AXS—priced at $10,500, $7,500, and $5,500, respectively.

All three builds use the same frame; Colnago doesn’t substitute a lower-grade frame on any build kits. The frame is 2x-compatible, but Colnago ships all builds with 1x13 groupsets.

The Red and Force models come with a wider-flare version of the brand’s in-house one-piece carbon cockpit, while the Rival model uses a traditional bar and stem. The Force and Rival bikes feature Vision TC45 carbon wheels, and the Red model ships with Zipp 303 XPLR SWs.

The only notable component “miss” on the G5-X bikes is the lack of power meters. All three tiers use SRAM cranksets with a 40T ring and 10-46T cassette, but oddly, none are power-equipped. In an age when riders of all disciplines and ability levels are data-hungry, a power meter is practically required equipment—especially at the Red AXS level.

Colnago’s G5-X sizing is numbered (45, 48, 51, 54, and 57), not t-shirt size-style (XS, S, M, L, and XL). But those numbers don’t exactly correspond to traditional metric frame sizing, so triple-check your measurements and Colnago’s geometry charts. Colnago dealers are often very knowledgeable about the brand and its nuances. But when in doubt, get a proper bike fit to be sure you are on the correct size.

Overall, the G5-X is an excellent bicycle. But this isn’t the bike for you if you want the gravel bike with the most tire clearance, every gear-carrying option, or the lowest price. Plenty of other bicycles hit any or all of those points, and they will ride great.

The G5-X rides beautifully and does the things a good gravel bike should do in 2026. It has a few deficiencies, but they probably aren’t deal-breakers for most riders who will want this bike. Riders will seek out the G5-X because the name on the downtube practically guarantees it goes very fast and handles beautifully—price will most likely be a distant consideration. After all, no one buys a Ferrari because it’s a “good deal”; they buy it for the brand’s heritage, prestige, and what it signifies.

The same goes for Colnago. You can buy a gravel bike with more tire clearance than the G5-X. You can also buy a lower-priced gravel bike, or one with a power meter, hidden bag mounts, and the exact tires you want. But none of those other bikes are a Colnago, and that’s what actually matters.

Although Ernesto Colnago sold a majority share of his fabled company to an Abu Dhabi-based investment fund in 2020, Colnago bikes are still special. In an era of look-alike frames, most bikes still don’t match Colnago’s ride quality and refinement. And sure, maybe some of that is mystique or hype. Many artists can paint beautiful pictures you can hang in your home; only a select group of masters’ artwork hangs in the Uffizi Gallery.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.
