#8961. Stop Cramming Bikes in Your Car. These 10 Editor-Tested Hitch Racks Make Hauling Easier and More Secure

Our editors hauled bikes for thousands of miles to find the easiest, sturdiest hitch racks.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Cramming your bike into your car or SUV gets old quickly. Removing wheels and getting mud or grease all over your interior is no fun, and transporting your bike inside your car also leaves less room for passengers, luggage, or gear. Hitch-mount racks are the easiest, most secure way to carry your bike to your riding destination without mess or hassle. They’re ideal for heading to your local mountain bike trails, taking a road trip with friends, or going for weekend rides with your kids.

Hitch racks mount to the receiver on your vehicle’s bumper, making hitch racks easier to load than roof racks—hoisting a heavy bike onto an SUV’s roof after a long ride is never fun. Plus, you don’t need to remove your front wheel. Unlike roof racks, you can also drive into parking garages and drive-thrus with bikes on a hitch rack. And importantly, in an era of sky-high fuel prices, hitch racks typically impact your gas mileage less than roof-mounted options.

While hitch racks usually cost more than simple, low-cost trunk-mount racks, they can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. Hitch-mount carriers can also carry heavier bikes, like electric bikes or full suspension rigs, than trunk racks and are more stable at highway speeds.

Our editors and test team evaluated dozens of hitch racks to see which ones perform best. Our staff has used some of these racks on their own vehicles for years, safely transporting bikes over tens of thousands of miles. Our picks for the best hitch-mounted bike racks vary in features like position, trunk access functionality, bike capacity, and price—but all are dependable options for your next cycling trip.

Based on price, weight capacity, and ease of use, Thule’s Outpace ranks as our current Best Overall pick. The Outpace is lighter and more compact than most hitch racks, which makes it easy to install and remove. At only 28 pounds, it’s light enough to carry across the garage and slide into the receiver tube. Setup takes less than a minute, so you can mount it on the car when you need to haul your bikes (rather than it semi-permanently living on your bumper).

The rack can accommodate a wider range of bike wheel sizes, making it great for families. The rack adapts easily to any size bicycle in either position. The tradeoff for this versatility is that it takes a bit longer to load than bulkier racks with cinch-style clamps. But for something that can carry all of our bikes, and is so quick to install or remove that it never has to be a permanent fixture, that’s a small price to pay.

Our tester noted the Outpace’s receiver arm is on the short side. It fit snugly against the bumper with about two inches to spare, but on another vehicle, it wouldn’t fit without a hitch extender.

The Trail Rider is a great, lower-cost alternative to premium racks. It holds two bikes in fixed wheel mounts, secured with a single ratcheting arm that clamps down over the frame. The upright beam (which holds the frame holders) folds back and out of the way for trunk access; it’s also handy for loading up two bikes. We could fold it down, set a bike on the rack closest to the car without lifting it up and over the arm, then lift the arm back into place and position the second bike.

The trade-off for the Trail Rider’s low price isn’t stability or strength, but adjustability: The bikes are positioned in a fixed location. You have limited ability to separate them if two bikes don’t fit well together. That said, you can stagger the wheel cradles so the bars and saddles don’t interfere.

The Swagman XTC2 is one of the most affordable 2-bike racks we recommend. This no-frills rack is a solid choice for budget-conscious riders. It fits both 1¼-inch and 2-inch receiver tubes, and it accommodates wheel sizes from 20 to 29 inches. However, with a total weight capacity of 70 pounds (35 pounds per bike), it’s not suitable for e-bikes.

As expected at this price, the rack has some trade-offs. The wheel hoops are adjustable, but not as smoothly or precisely as on more premium racks. The rack doesn’t tilt away from the vehicle when loaded, limiting access to tailgates or liftgates. Lastly, you must remove the center support bar to load a bike on the inside tray.

Yet, the XTC2 is lightweight, durable, and very reasonably priced. If you’re willing to trade a bit of convenience for significant savings, the Swagman XTC2 is a reliable and practical option.

The Piston Pro X is our runner-up for Best Overall hitch rack; its construction, features, and style make it a standout pick in the category. Aside from the high price, the Piston Pro X is almost the perfect hitch rack for most users.

With the Piston Pro X, Küat elevated the rack from something purely utilitarian to a desirable piece of gear that’s easier to use than other racks. The rack includes smart features (such as integrated brake and turn-signal lights) and can carry more wheel sizes (and more weight) than almost any other rack on the market.

The top-end Pro X model costs more than almost any other hitch-mount rack, but it has proven extremely durable and maintains its good looks. It's also available in 3- and 4-bike models. Küat also offers a slightly cheaper Piston Pro variant, which ditches the Kashima coating on the pistons and the integrated brake lights and turn signals.

If you like the Küat racks but $1,600 is out of your price range, the brand offers several other hitch-style racks that could meet your needs. One great option is the Sherpa 2.0 model.

While the Sherpa doesn’t have the features or carrying capacity of Küat’s more expensive racks, it has two big upsides—color options and low weight. The Sherpa weighs only 32 pounds (claimed) in the 2-inch hitch configuration (1.25-in. also available). Küat offers the Sherpa in three colors: black metallic (with a silver accent), grey metallic (with orange), and pearl white (with silver).

The Sherpa carries two bicycles weighing up to 40 pounds per tray. So it’s ideal for non-electric road, gravel, and mountain bikes. It has an integrated cable lock to secure your bikes during rest stops or meal breaks, and it features a foot-operated lever to lower the rack into position for loading bikes.

It’s often difficult to carry e-bikes that are equipped with racks and fenders on traditional hitch racks. That’s because many hitch racks secure the bike with extending arms that clamp one or both wheels. However, Thule’s EasyFold XT model holds your bike by its frame.

Another feature that makes the EasyFold ideal for e-bike owners is the included ramp. This makes loading or removing your bikes much easier; no more wrestling with heavy bikes or front wheels or handlebars flopping as you load them onto the rack. And the ramp attaches to the rack when you’re finished.

Thanks to the rack’s 45-pound weight, it’s easy to remove it from your vehicle when you’re not using it. It folds down and features casters (which make moving it around your garage easier). The EasyFold XT’s biggest drawback is that Thule only rates it to 65 pounds per bike. While that will accommodate many e-bikes, some fat tire models may weigh too much.

When Thule debuted the T2 over a decade ago, it raised the bar for what cyclists expect from a hitch-mounted bike rack. Over the years, Thule updated the rack to accommodate wider tires and different wheel sizes. It also improved the T2’s look and made it easier to operate. One of the best recent upgrades is a wide-trigger handle that allows you to raise and lower the rack (and dip it out of the way for access to rear hatches) with one hand.

Integrated cable locks help keep your bikes secure for quick stops, and each tray can hold a bicycle up to 60 pounds and tires up to 5 inches wide. This makes the T2 a good option for all but the heaviest e-bikes. The T2 Pro’s arms have wide, comfortable grips that slide easily to secure the front wheel. Instead of using a bolt, the rack secures to your hitch receiver with an expansion wedge that tightens with a locking knob. The system makes installing and removing the T2 easier (though it weighs 52 pounds), but it’s not foolproof.

Yakima’s StageTwo two-bike rack goes head-to-head with premium offerings from Küat and Thule at a lower price. In about 2,500 miles of on-car testing, the StageTwo impressed us with its ease of use and flex-free performance. This rack is only rated up to 35 pounds per tray, so it’s not made for transporting e-bikes. However, it’s one of only two racks on this list that accommodates wheels as small as 16 inches.

The StageTwo’s trays are offset, which means less chance of contact when carrying two similarly sized bikes (however, bikes sit more widely apart, so watch those tight parking spaces). The rack includes two SKS locking cables (they don’t auto-retract, so tuck them back in when not in use). The StageTwo also includes an integrated lock loop for extra security when parked or locking your rack off the vehicle.

The rack is offered in 1.25- and 2-inch sizes. The 2-inch variant can accommodate four bikes with an add-on kit. Also, check Yakima’s fit guide before buying—One of our testers experienced a hardware fitment issue.

If you travel to mountain resort towns (or have been around trailheads or bike parks lately), you’ve probably seen behemoth racks like these on the back of vans and trucks. Since modern mountain bikes are bulky, racks like Thule’s ReVert make sense if you’re hauling a full load with a single vehicle.

The ReVert holds six bikes, loads quickly, and sticks out no farther than a standard 2-bike horizontal rack. Its carrying capacity makes it ideal for large families, race teams, or ride groups.

At over 87 pounds, the ReVert is undeniably heavy. However, a few smart features make the rack manageable. Dual hydraulic dampers assist with lowering the rack when it’s fully loaded, so you don’t have to wrestle with it. Once in the lowered position, even shorter riders and kids can lift their bikes high enough to slot them into the baskets. Individual bikes are spaced 11 inches apart, giving you plenty of room to carry any combination—flat bar, drop bar, even cruisers.

1UP USA has built a cult-like following with its industrial-looking racks that take a simplistic approach to securing your bike. This model features two ratcheting arms that clamp down on your wheels—no hooks or straps necessary.

The Equip-D’s pivot mechanism is smooth and reliable even after years of abuse (although an occasional shot of WD-40 White Lithium Grease Spray goes a long way in keeping the release mechanism running smoothly). A T-handle release positioned at the end of the hitch bar means you don’t need to reach through the rack to fold it up. Tiered trays position bikes closer together, and the rack rides out of the way of most exhaust pipes. 1Up also offers the Equip in a single-bike version for a sleeker look.

Hitch racks are bicycle carriers that attach to your vehicle’s hitch receiver. Popular models carry one to four bikes, but some hanging-style hitch racks can haul up to six bikes.

A hitch is a standard feature on most trucks and many SUVs. However, if you have a car or wagon, a hitch can often be added. If your vehicle doesn’t already have a receiver, it’s easy to have one installed. (U-Haul is a reliable and affordable option for installation.)Receivers come in two sizes: 1¼-inch and 2-inch (measured across the inside of the square opening). Most trucks and SUVs use a 2-inch receiver. Many racks are available in both sizes, but heavier-duty racks—and racks that carry three or more bikes—often require the larger 2-inch receiver for added strength and stability. Racks rated to carry heavyweight e-bikes also typically require a 2-inch receiver.

If the rack will live on your vehicle year-round or see frequent use, invest in the most durable model your budget allows. While all racks listed here secure bikes effectively, higher-priced options tend to have sturdier moving parts—ratchets, straps, buckles, and locks—that stand up better to long-term use.

Not all hitch racks are rated for the extra weight of e-bikes. Those that aren’t suited for heavier bikes are clearly noted in our reviews.

Some racks are quite heavy, which contributes to their strength but can be inconvenient if you plan to remove and reinstall the rack frequently.

For most vehicles—aside from sedans—accessing the trunk or tailgate is restricted when the rack is in use or folded up. Many of our top picks offer tilt-down designs that allow you to open the back of your vehicle even with bikes loaded. For full access, swing-away adapters like the Küat Pivot v2 Swing-Away allow the entire rack to pivot 90 degrees, completely clearing the rear of your car or truck.

Need more clearance? Sometimes a simple hitch extender can do the trick. For added stability and peace of mind, we also recommend using an anti-rattle clamp with any rack you choose.

Pros: Hitch racks strike the perfect balance between the ease of access of a trunk rack and the security of a quality roof rack. They slot into your car’s hitch receiver, relying on no flimsy straps or sketchy hooks. They’re also positioned behind your car, which is great for gas mileage and roof-collision prevention (low standing height). Better yet, many are modular, allowing you to add extra trays, locks, and even bottle openers for more personalized functionality.

Cons: These racks are the most consistently expensive out there—quality materials and a confidence-inspiring construction unquestionably affect their price. Furthermore, they can be a pain to remove, as most options weigh well over 40 pounds and need tools to detach. Furthermore, with bikes on the rack, they add significant length to your vehicle, which could prove tricky if you need to parallel park. And most critically, not every car has a hitch, which means you’ll either need to install one yourself or forego this style entirely.

Our editors drove hundreds (and in some cases, thousands) of miles with their bikes on these racks. We hauled road bikes, mountain bikes, e-bikes, and city bikes. We carried bikes with disc brakes, big wheels, and fat tires. Our test team used these racks for months, in various environments and conditions. We tested them in the salty winters of Pennsylvania, the high mountains of Colorado, and the gritty Arizona desert.

These racks in this story stand out for their ease of installation and use, lack of play in key areas, manageable weight, and bike capacity. We also looked for sharp prices and deals.

Whether you’re a roadie on the way to your next fondo, a mountain biker heading to the trailhead, or loading up the family for a weekend adventure, our rack picks will cover whatever needs you and your riding crew may have.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8960. Triathlon Gear Our Editors Used and Loved in October 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

It’s officially the off-season. In Ohio, we’re having the best fall, where no one complains about the weather (rare for Ohioans) and no wind or rain storms have blown through, robbing us of the vibrant change in the leaves. Hiking is a staple way to enjoy the crunchy leaves, swimming has moved fully indoors, and biking has a sort of leisure to it that it doesn’t have when the landscape is green.

As we slow down and explore other outdoor hobbies in the coming months, here’s a look at the gear our editors are reaching for.

This might seem like an unusual choice for a triathlete, but as the race season winds down and we transition from workouts to just-getting-out, I find myself blasting all of my tempo trainers to the back of my closet in favor of this pair of Jeep-wheel-level all-terrain crushers. For those unfamiliar with Norda, the Canadian brand hit the scene in 2021 (bad timing, sorry) with the release of their ultra-premium — read: ultra-expensive — $285 shoe dubbed the 001. Folks had a field day with the high price, but few could deny that the 001 was something different than what was out there already.

Fast forward to today, and Norda is still (crazy) expensive, but they also still offer shoes that are entirely novel in the increasingly crowded trail running shoe world. The 055 was released earlier this summer as a maximal take on the well-loved, but race-focused 005. For me, I love how you can point your foot at literally anything and the thick-but-stable base will eat it up. Better yet, the woven gaiter adds another layer of stability and protection, meaning you don’t really have to think much about where you put your feet, allowing me to, quite simply, zone out and enjoy the view. And that’s what fall “training” is all about, anyway.

Winter is coming, which in Phoenix means two things: socks come out of storage, and they better be day-glo. Because I live and train downtown, where traffic is abundant and drivers are always (always!) distracted, I dress as obnoxiously as possible to make sure they see me. That means neon fabrics, reflective materials, and LED lights on as many points as possible.

Years ago, I interviewed a safety expert who said you especially want these materials on the parts of your body that move he most when you ride or run, as movement is more likely to catch the eye of a driver. These bright socks have reflective yarn woven into the fabric, making my legs easier to spot on rides and runs. They’re comfortable, they stay up, and they stand up to multiple runs and laundry cycles each week.

Do I look like a 90s fever dream in my neon wardrobe? I sure do. But you’ll see me coming from a mile away, and that’s the whole point.

I haven’t had long hair in the 14 years I’ve been a triathlete — until now. I hate the feeling of hair skimming my neck or swishing back and forth as I run, so it has to be all the way up in the ugliest messy bun. Basically, I’m the opposite of Marjolaine Pierré.

I found that the Goody ComforFlex holds my hair well without pulling, no matter the intensity of workouts. And I don’t end up with tons of hair wrapped around them, which leads me to believe they are keeping my hair at least somewhat healthy despite regular chlorine exposure and frequent washes.

They’ve also held up well, so I can use the same one for at least a month before replacing it.

I’m ashamed to admit I’ve been one of *those* triathletes showing up at the local bike shop, frazzled and looking for the nearest mechanic, then frantically explaining how my seat clamp fell down my downtube and lodged itself somewhere seemingly impossible to reach. Yes, this happened to me at Ironman Chattanooga last year. As someone who prides myself on fixing my own bike issues, this was and still is my worst nightmare.

But I know I’m not alone. Between packing and trying to fit in final workouts ahead of travel, we triathletes can make some poor choices. Add to it that we’re limited in what tools we can bring to fix the problems we create, and it’s a recipe for disaster. Even when we have room and enough weight left to throw them in the bag, we often rush the pack job and toss them in without much organization.

After Chattanooga, I vowed to be more prepared. That’s when a friend showed me this trusty little roll-up tool bag that they use for camping. Small enough that it doesn’t take up all the room, big enough to fit what I need, and cheap enough to buy one for myself and a friend. It was the perfect recommendation.

And the best thing is you don’t have to travel for triathlon to get use out of it. Mine hangs in the garage when I’m home, and I use it every time I work on my bike.

— Travis Mundell, social media strategist

#8957. That Mysterious Bike Creak Is Driving You Crazy—Here’s How to Check Your Bottom Bracket

Simple checks to pinpoint bottom bracket creaks before they become bigger repairs.

As cyclists, we hear a lot of sounds when riding. Usually, the noises come from chirping birds, the wind rustling leaves, or your bike’s tires rolling over your favorite trail. But sometimes the noises sound bad and come from your bike, and those noises can range from annoying to anxiety-inducing as you ponder the cause.

Bicycle components are moving parts that wear out and sometimes need adjustment. These squeaks, creaks, clicks, and other strange sounds are often a sign that something on your bike needs repair or replacement. And if your bike seems extra noisy, it might be time for some routine maintenance.

Noises on bikes are sometimes frustrating and mysterious. It’s often a challenge to figure out exactly where the sound originates—especially if it’s hard to reproduce when not riding. When I ran a shop, we would have customers come in and they would be certain that a noise was coming from one spot—only to find the culprit be somewhere else. Many times a noise would originate at the cranks or bottom bracket, so that’s what we’ll focus on here.

It’s worth checking on the lowest hanging fruit before we dig into the bottom bracket. The most common noisemakers are loose parts or bearings requiring adjustment, cleaning, or replacement. Performing regular preride bolt checks helps keep components tight and noises at bay. Several spots on your bike use bearings to rotate smoothly, including your headset, bottom bracket, hubs, and suspension linkages on mountain bikes. Keep these bearings properly adjusted to cut down on squeaks and knocking sounds.

Before checking if the noise originates from your bottom bracket, check that the crank bolts (which affix the crank arms to the BB on many bikes) are sufficiently tight. You might hear a clicking when these bolts loosen. And if a crank bolt entirely backs out, it can cause a crankarm to fall off while riding or damage your crank or frame. Grab a torque wrench and tighten the bolts to the manufacturer’s recommended specification.

After you are sure the noise is not from a loose crankarm, stand next to your bike and grab both brakes. Then, put your foot on the pedal closest to you and press inward. If the bike still creaks or ticks when you put weight on the pedal, the problem likely comes from your bottom bracket.

If the clicking sound isn’t from your drivetrain or pedals (see below), your BB may be loose, or the bearings may be worn. Many bikes use a non-adjustable cartridge or press-fit BB that must be replaced when the bearings wear out. Some systems (such as SRAM DUB and Race Face Cinch) use a preload ring to add preload to the bottom bracket bearings. These rings can loosen and cause a click while pedaling. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions to tighten it back up.

If you don’t hear anything, the problem is likely the bearings in your headset, hubs, or suspension parts. Bearings can wear out after a season, especially if you live somewhere wet or sandy. Your local bike shop can help you order and install new ones.

It’s also possible you simply need a new bottom bracket in the bike. Bottom bracket standards are a deep rabbit hole and can feel overly complex if you aren’t familiar with the system. Different frames and different cranks require different bottom brackets. Before searching Amazon for the best deal on bottom brackets, consult the technical specifications for your specific bike and component group or visit your local shop for direction.

I have seen bottom bracket issues actually cause issues on carbon frames as well. I’ve seen this specifically on older carbon frames with press-fit bottom brackets that were not maintained over time. All the bikes that I saw frame issues from bottom brackets fell into the same category: older carbon road bikes with press-fit bottom brackets that were not maintained for years. Eventually the customer would hear a noise, but keep riding. Then that noise would turn into knocking in the crank. By the time they got to our shop, the space in the frame for the bottom bracket was no longer a perfect circle. That circle shifted into an oval over time—which more times than not resulted in a new frame being needed. If you have a creak in your bottom bracket, get it checked out (or inspect it yourself) before it becomes something bigger.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

Picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

Here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Now let's talk about how you actually get those miles into your account.

The primary transfer path the ChooseFI community uses is American Express Membership Rewards → HawaiianMiles at a 1:1 ratio. If you have the Amex Gold, Platinum, or a no-annual-fee Amex Everyday card earning MR points, you can transfer directly to Hawaiian. Transfer speed is 1–2 days — not instant, so plan accordingly and don't wait until the last minute.

Two other paths exist if you're working with different currencies:

One critical nuance: HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, not credit card spend. Hawaiian does have a co-branded credit card, but it's not a top earner for most people's daily spend. This means your primary accumulation strategy is transfer partners — Amex MR and Bilt are your best levers.

Another key detail: Hawaiian miles never expire. This matters because you can slowly accumulate miles across multiple statement cycles, transfer when you're ready to book, and not feel rushed. There's no expiration clock running against you.

Finally, the no fuel surcharges policy is a genuine differentiator. Many programs — particularly those involving European carriers — tack on $300–$600 in surcharges that gut your redemption's net value. HawaiianMiles charges no fuel surcharges on Hawaiian-operated flights. Your 7,500 miles covers the flight. Taxes and fees on interisland tickets are minimal, often just a few dollars. What you see is what you get.

Go to hawaiianairlines.com and use the 'Book' tool, selecting 'Reward Travel' as your travel type. Enter your route — for example, HNL to OGG (Honolulu to Kahului, Maui) or HNL to LIH (Honolulu to Lihue, Kauai). Plug in your desired travel date and search. You're looking for economy award space priced at 7,500 miles. Availability on interisland routes is almost always wide open — this is one of the best availability scores (5/5) of any sweet spot in this guide series, but it costs nothing to confirm before you transfer.

If you don't have a HawaiianMiles account, create one at hawaiianairlines.com — it takes about two minutes and is free. Note your HawaiianMiles number. You'll need it for the transfer step.

From Amex Membership Rewards: Log into your Amex account, navigate to 'Membership Rewards,' select 'Transfer Points,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines HawaiianMiles as the destination. Enter your HawaiianMiles number and the number of miles you want to transfer (at minimum, 7,500 per person you're booking). Transfers process in 1–2 days.

From Bilt Rewards: Log into your Bilt app or biltrewards.com, navigate to 'Redeem,' select 'Transfer to Airline Partner,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines at 1:1. Same 1–2 day transfer window.

From Marriott Bonvoy: Use this only as a last resort due to the 3:1 ratio. Navigate to Bonvoy's transfer portal and select HawaiianMiles. Allow up to 5 days.

Once your miles land (check your HawaiianMiles account balance), return to hawaiianairlines.com, log in, and re-run your award search. Select the flight you want, confirm the 7,500-mile price, and proceed through checkout. Taxes on interisland awards are typically just a few dollars — no fuel surcharges apply.

HawaiianMiles opens its booking window 330 days out. If you're planning a Hawaii trip far in advance and have specific flight times in mind, you can search and book early. That said, given the excellent availability on these routes, booking 2–4 weeks out is usually fine.

This is rare for interisland routes, but if it happens, try: searching adjacent dates, looking at different departure times on the same route, or checking alternate routing (e.g., OGG to LIH instead of HNL to LIH directly). Interisland availability doesn't fluctuate the way transatlantic business class does.

Let's make this concrete. You're planning a two-week Hawaii trip for two people. You've booked your Honolulu arrival flight separately, and now you need to connect the dots between islands: Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) mid-trip, and then Maui (OGG) to Lihue, Kauai (LIH) before heading home.

The cash price check: Pull up hawaiianairlines.com and look at what these tickets retail for. On a typical mid-trip travel day, the HNL→OGG segment is priced at $189 per person. The OGG→LIH hop runs $149 per person. For two travelers, that's $676 in cash — before you've bought a single plate of shave ice.

The points price: Each segment costs 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person in economy. Two passengers, two flights: 30,000 HawaiianMiles total, plus roughly $10–$20 in taxes and fees across both bookings. No fuel surcharges.

The CPP calculation: You're replacing $676 in cash spending with 30,000 miles. That's 2.25 cents per point — well above the 0.8–1.2 cpp you'd expect on typical HawaiianMiles redemptions, and solidly within the 1.3–3.3 cpp sweet spot range for this redemption.

What the experience looks like: Hawaiian's interisland product is no-frills — these are 20-to-40-minute flights on Boeing 717s. You won't get a meal or premium service. But you will get a reliable, on-time carrier, clean aircraft, and the undeniable satisfaction of hopping between two of the most beautiful island destinations on Earth without opening your wallet at the gate.

For the ChooseFI traveler, the win isn't the in-flight experience — it's the mental accounting shift. You budgeted for interisland flights; now that budget goes to a sunset sailing charter or a snorkeling excursion instead. The points paid for the planes. The cash funds the memories.

Do: Transfer Points in the Right Batch Size HawaiianMiles doesn't allow you to transfer partial miles back out, so calculate exactly how many you need before initiating a transfer. For two passengers on two flights, that's 30,000 miles. Transfer exactly that amount — or a small buffer — rather than dumping your entire MR balance into a program you may not use frequently.

Do: Use Amex MR or Bilt as Your Primary Earning Strategy Since HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, your accumulation plan should center on transferable currencies. The Amex Gold Card (4x on dining and groceries) and Amex Platinum (5x on flights) are elite MR earners. Bilt's no-annual-fee card earning on rent is underused by the ChooseFI community for exactly this kind of transfer.

Do: Search for Availability Before You Transfer This is worth repeating as a pro tip because new points travelers make this mistake constantly. Transfer speeds are 1–2 days for Amex MR and Bilt. Don't transfer points and then discover the flight you wanted is sold out. Always confirm availability first, then transfer, then book immediately once miles land.

Avoid: Using Marriott Bonvoy for This Transfer At a 3:1 ratio, you'd spend 22,500 Bonvoy points for a 7,500-mile award. Bonvoy points are worth approximately 0.7–0.9 cpp on their own best redemptions. The math doesn't hold here — save your Bonvoy points for hotel redemptions.

Do: Consider the Merger Context Hawaiian Airlines is in the process of merging with Alaska Airlines, and HawaiianMiles may eventually transition into Alaska Mileage Plan. Pay attention to program announcements. This could change transfer partners, award pricing, or program structure. The current sweet spot exists now — book it while the program operates under its current rules.

Avoid: Waiting for a 'Better' Redemption on These Miles HawaiianMiles are a limited-use currency. They're excellent for interisland and mainland-to-Hawaii flights, but they don't transfer to other airlines and don't unlock international business class sweet spots. If you've got miles in this program, use them for exactly what they're designed for — Hawaiian flights — rather than letting them sit hoping for a better opportunity that may never come.

Do: Book Multiple Segments in a Single Trip If you're doing a true multi-island itinerary, every interisland hop is 7,500 miles. Three islands means two hops — 15,000 miles per person. Plan your island sequence to minimize backtracking, and book all segments at once once your miles transfer.

Make multi-island trips affordable with the right points strategy

Most visitors to Hawaii stick to one island because interisland flights add $100-$400+ per person to the trip cost. By using points for these short hops, you unlock a fundamentally different Hawaii experience — island-hopping from Oahu to Maui to the Big Island to Kauai without the airfare costs stacking up. This is a multiplier strategy: you are not just saving on one flight, you are enabling an entirely different type of trip. Combining a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight with points-funded interisland hops creates a nearly free (in cash) multi-island Hawaiian vacation.

Decide which islands you want to visit and in what order. The most common combinations are Oahu + Maui, Oahu + Big Island, or a three-island itinerary. Map out how many interisland hops you need so you know the total points required.

Check Hawaiian Airlines (7,500 miles each way), Southwest (variable, typically 4,000-8,000 points), and United (5,000-7,500 miles) for each interisland segment. Southwest often offers the best flexibility with no change fees and no blackout dates.

For Hawaiian Airlines, transfer Amex Membership Rewards. For Southwest, earn Rapid Rewards directly or transfer from Chase (transfer to Southwest is currently limited). For United segments, transfer from Chase or use Turkish Miles&Smiles for even lower pricing.

Book each interisland hop as a separate one-way award. This gives you maximum flexibility to mix airlines and optimize pricing per segment. One-way awards have no penalty compared to round trips on these short routes.

Align your interisland hops with your arrival and departure flights. Arrive on one island and depart from a different one (open-jaw booking) to avoid backtracking. For example, arrive Honolulu, hop to Maui, depart Maui to the mainland.

Hawaiian Airlines has the most extensive interisland network and offers the most daily frequencies. Southwest Airlines also operates key interisland routes (Honolulu-Maui, Honolulu-Kona, Honolulu-Lihue). United flies select interisland segments as well. Each airline has different award pricing and transfer partner access.

Hawaiian Airlines interisland awards typically price at 7,500 HawaiianMiles each way. Southwest varies by cash fare but generally costs 4,000-8,000 Rapid Rewards points each way for interisland hops. United interisland segments can be booked for 5,000-7,500 miles using various Star Alliance partner programs.

Yes, especially when booking multiple hops. A family of four making two interisland hops at $150 each way would spend $1,200 in cash. Converting that to points frees up significant cash for accommodations, activities, and dining. The per-point value (1.5-2.5 cents) is reasonable, and the trip flexibility gained is substantial.

A popular strategy is to fly into Honolulu (Oahu), hop to Maui for beaches and Haleakala, then continue to the Big Island (Kona) for volcanoes and snorkeling, and optionally finish on Kauai for dramatic scenery. Each hop is 30-60 minutes. Allow 2-3 days minimum per island.

This redemption was built for families and couples planning a multi-island Hawaii vacation — full stop. If you're visiting multiple islands (which most Hawaii first-timers and repeat visitors do), you're already mentally budgeting for interisland flights. This sweet spot simply redirects that cash budget back into your pocket and replaces it with points.

Families get a 5/5 Family Friendly score here for good reason: availability is wide open, booking is simple, and the economics scale beautifully. Four people, two hops = 60,000 miles to cover potentially $1,200+ in interisland airfare. That's an extraordinary displacement of vacation cash.

Beginners are explicitly welcomed by this redemption's design. There's no partner airline complexity, no fuel surcharge math to calculate, no routing rules to decode. You search on Hawaiian's website, you transfer points, you book. The 5/5 Beginner Friendly and Easy to Book scores reflect that this is genuinely one of the simplest award redemptions you can execute.

Minimum points needed: 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person per segment. For a solo traveler doing two hops, that's 15,000 miles. For a family of four doing two hops, that's 60,000 miles.

This is NOT for: Travelers who don't have an Amex MR or Bilt account and no path to earning HawaiianMiles quickly. It's also not ideal for travelers who only need a single interisland flight — the opportunity cost of setting up the transfer relationship for 7,500 miles may not be worth it unless you're already accumulating MR points for other redemptions.

This redemption earns a **Beginner** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. In a world of waitlists, fuel surcharges, routing rules, and phone-only bookings, Hawaiian interisland awards are refreshingly clean. **What makes it easy:** Award availability is consistently excellent (5/5). The booking portal is functional and user-friendly. There are no fuel surcharges to calculate. Miles never expire, so there's no pressure. You can complete the entire redemption — from transfer initiation to confirmed booking — in about 48 hours. **The one genuine friction point:** Earning HawaiianMiles isn't as straightforward as earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex MR. Hawaiian doesn't have a widely-used co-branded credit card for most people's everyday spend. This means you're dependent on transfer partners, and the Amex MR and Bilt paths are your primary options. If you don't have either, this redemption becomes harder to access. **Tip 1:** Start with an Amex card that earns Membership Rewards — the Amex Gold is the ChooseFI community favorite for everyday earning. Once you're accumulating MR points, you have a direct path to Hawaiian via a 1:1 transfer. **Tip 2:** Always search award availability before transferring. It takes 30 seconds and protects you from the one mistake that could derail an otherwise smooth booking. **Tip 3:** Don't overthink the merger situation. Hawaiian and Alaska remain separate programs today. Book what's in front of you. If you can earn Amex MR points, you can execute this redemption. It's the perfect first award booking for a ChooseFI member who wants to see how the system works without risking complexity.

Interisland awards are the key that unlocks multi-island Hawaii vacations without the stacking airfare costs that keep most travelers on a single island. At 7,500-10,000 miles per hop, the points cost is modest, and the trip transformation is significant. Whether you use Hawaiian Airlines miles, Southwest Rapid Rewards, or United partner programs, the strategy is the same: let points handle the short hops so your cash stays in your pocket for experiences. Combined with a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight, interisland awards make a multi-island Hawaiian vacation one of the most achievable aspirational trips in travel rewards.

#8954. 5 Yin Yoga Poses for (Practically) Instant Calm

Katie McGrath is a certified yin yoga instructor. She leads classes on her YouTube channel, Yin Yoga with Katie, and offers invaluable advice on YJ as well. Here, she shares five yin yoga poses to help relieve stress so you can find calmness.

Some days bring more stress than others. Perhaps you have stopped (or have yet to start) working yet your jaw is tight, your breath sits high in your chest, and lying down does nothing except give your mind a quiet room in which to be loud.

Yin yoga is useful here for one very practical reason: yin yoga poses hold you close to the ground for several minutes. There is nothing to coordinate and nothing to balance. That combination gives your body and mind—and, more specifically, your nervous system—time to register that you’re in a safe place to release stress, which is something that, depending on you and your circumstances, a faster practice doesn’t always accomplish.

Stay in each of the following yin yoga poses for 3 to 5 minutes—and remember that a longer hold is not necessarily “better.” Aim for roughly 50 to 60 percent of the sensation you could create, which is a line in the sand rather than something carved in stone. If a pose feels exceptionally loud in your body, back off.

As you hold each pose encourage your exhale to become longer than your inhale. This is a simple and effective way to trigger your parasympathetic nervous system. In between the poses, lie flat for about a minute. You can stay still and do nothing or wiggle your body, it’s your choice. That minute is part of the practice, not just a gap in between the poses.

Practicing yoga for stress is not a cure. Instead, it is a way of placing your body in a position where settling down becomes a lot more likely. You might not feel dramatically different, and that is fine. Calm usually feels quieter than we expect it to be. What you are really after is a body that is slightly less braced than it was prior to your practice.

Gather what you have: a bolster or a firm cushion, two blankets, one or two yoga blocks, and a wall. If you have an eye pillow, feel free to use it.

What it does: This is a gentle, fully supported version of Child’s Pose that crosses into restorative yoga, a close cousin of yin yoga. The head makes contact with something solid, which many people find settling on its own. This shape also closes the body inward, which is useful when you want less input rather than more.

How to: Kneel with your knees wide and your big toes touching. Place a bolster lengthways between your thighs and lie your torso down over it. Turn your head to one side. Halfway through your hold, turn it the other way to stretch your neck evenly.

Add more props: Place a block under the far end of the bolster for more support and something solid to rest your head on. If your hips do not reach your heels, add a folded blanket between your calves and your backside, or place a yoga block under your hips. If your knees object to the shape of this pose, lie on your back and hug your knees toward your chest instead. For a more stretch-focused, yin yoga version of this pose, try it without the props.

Hold: Stay here for a total of 4 minutes, two with your head facing each direction.

What it does: This supine twist releases the lower back and the outer hips. And because you are on your back, it asks almost nothing of you but to surrender to gravity.

How to: Lie on your back. Draw both knees toward your chest, then let them fall toward the right. Take your arms out wide. Let your head turn toward the left, if that is comfortable, or keep it neutral as you face the ceiling.

Add props: Place a bolster or folded blanket underneath the knees, if needed, so that they land on something supportive rather than hanging in space. If your right shoulder lifts off the floor, prop it with a folded blanket instead of constantly forcing it toward the mat. If your lower back complains, lower the knees less close to the ground.

Hold: Stay here for 3 minutes on each side.

What it does: This supported backbend opens your chest and ribcage, which both spend most of the day closed. When the chest is open in Fish Pose, your breath can expand more freely.

How to: Place a yoga block on its lowest level behind you on the mat. For more support, have a second block ready to rest your head on. Lie back onto the block, aligning the bottom of your shoulder blades with one edge. Rest the back of your head on the second block or bring the crown of your head to the mat. Let your arms fall open at your sides. Keep your legs long or you can bend your knees and keep your feet on the mat.

Add props: Add a bolster underneath your knees or, for more of a hip stretch, touch the soles of the feet together and let your knees fall to the sides, tucking cushions underneath your outer thighs. If your lower back is uncomfortable, try lying back over a bolster placed lengthways instead. If your head tips back quite a lot and your throat feels exposed, add a small cushion underneath your head.

Hold: Stay here for 4 minutes. Come out slowly, and rest before you move on.

What it does: This shape offers lateral flexion, also known as a side stretch, which is the direction almost nobody moves during ordinary life. Banana Pose lengthens the body along your outer torso, including the muscles between the ribs, so that your ribcage has more room to expand when you breathe in.

How to: Lie on your back with your legs long. Before you move anything, notice that the backs of both hips are on the floor and level, and try to keep your hips in the center of the mat. Walk both feet to the right, as far as they’ll go without the right hip lifting. Reach your arms overhead and walk both hands toward the right, taking hold of your left wrist with your right hand if that is comfortable and available to you. If you want a more intense side stretch, cross your right ankle over your left. Soften your jaw and let the breath move into the long side of your body.

Add props: No props needed here! Skip the ankle cross if the outer hip is the loudest thing in the pose. If your arms do not want to go overhead, rest them wherever they are comfortable.

Hold: Stay here for 3 minutes on each side.

What it does: Legs Up the Wall finds the legs are supported and the spine is flat, so it is a good place to stop. It’s also one of the most effective restorative poses for activating your parasympathetic nervous system, allowing for real and accessible relaxation.

How to: Sit sideways with one hip against the wall, then swing your legs up as you lie back. Shuffle your backside close to the wall, or a few inches away if that suits your hamstrings better. Rest your hands on your belly or out to the sides.

Add props: For extra comfort, slide a folded blanket under your hips if your lower back feels flat and strained. If your feet tingle, bend your knees or come down for a moment.

Hold: Stay here for 5-10 minutes or for as long as you need.

Extract yourself from each shape slowly and with care. To finish your practice, find your way to a comfortable seat and breathe here with your eyes closed (or your gaze soft) for 1-3 minutes. Give yourself a moment before you reach for your phone.

#8953. Zipp’s Cheapest Carbon Wheelset Makes a Strong Case for Itself—But There’s One Catch

A major-brand carbon wheelset at a lower price, with a great warranty and one trade-off road riders should consider.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Zipp’s 404S replaces the 303S with a deeper 50mm rim for modern road riding. Zipp says the new profile saves about two watts over its predecessor. At $1,300 for the pair, the wheels bring a familiar name and a lifetime warranty to a price well below the brand’s flagship models.

I rode the 404S on my steel Ritchey Road Logic, logging roughly 800 miles over two months. They’re a totally fine, solid wheelset. They feel settled at speed without riding harshly, accelerate well once they’re rolling, and remain stable in gusty conditions. In other words, Zipp made a perfectly good wheelset that will likely come stock on many SRAM-equipped bikes.

On the road, the 404S fades into the background of your ride (in a good way). The wheels feel comfortable without feeling harsh. Get them up to speed, and they are reassuringly solid. In terms of crosswind performance, I’d rate them quite good. They aren’t quite on the level of something like a Roval Rapide CLX III (basically the gold standard for crosswind performance), but they still feel very stable even on a gusty day. Once I'm moving, they have the responsive feel I expect from a 50mm wheelset, whether I’m pedaling through a corner or getting back up to speed on a rolling road.

The weight shows up more on steep climbs or when accelerating out of a slow corner; these wheels don’t have the immediate, lively feel of lighter aero options. That doesn’t make them feel sluggish in normal riding; it’s just the clearest difference I noticed after riding lighter wheels.

Otherwise, I found little to separate the 404S from more expensive wheelsets with a similar rim depth. They do the basic job well: they feel stable in the wind, comfortable on imperfect roads, and once you’re up to speed, their weight disadvantage largely disappears.

The 404S uses a Tubeless Straight Side, or hookless, rim design. That means checking tire compatibility and pressure limits before you ride. Zipp recommends tires from 28 to 39mm, and says the wheels are optimized for 28–29mm tires for best aero performance, with a maximum pressure of 72.5 psi. Many riders might miss that if you run a 30 or 32mm road tire, the maximum pressure limit drops to 65 psi, according to ETRTO.

Those limits may not affect riders who already use wider tires at lower pressures. But I still see hookless as a miss for road wheels in 2026 for many reasons. Sure, a handful of high-profile issues in the pro peloton didn’t help, but neither did the steady drip of unease coming from inside the industry itself. While Zipp has stood behind the standard, I’d rather give the company credit for acknowledging that many riders (including me) would prefer a hooked option. instead of dealing with a relatively low max tire-pressure limit, consulting pressure charts, and reading tire-compatibility lists.

ENVE, arguably the biggest proponent of hookless road wheels, has already made this pivot. The brand's flagship racing models, the SES 4.5 and 6.7 Pro wheels, both feature a “mini hook.” This leaves only Zipp and Giant/Cadex sticking with hookless for now, and given my predictions earlier this year, I would guess both are at least considering their options.

At $1,300, the 404S sits between a few other 50mm carbon wheelsets. HUNT’s 50 Carbon Disc is listed at $1,249, with a 50mm rim, 22mm internal width, and a hooked tire interface. HUNT lists its weight at 1,464 grams, making it a close alternative for about $50 less, with a hooked rim.

Shimano’s Ultegra C50 is another 50mm option, listed at $1,570 for the pair. It has a hooked rim and a 21mm internal width, making it a little more expensive than the Zipp, with a narrower rim bed.

The harder comparison for Zipp is basically any wheel from Light Bicycle. Light Bicycle’s complete Airia wheel builds start at $1,144, and that base build is claimed to weigh 1,218 grams. The 55mm-deep test set weighed 1,101 grams without tape or valves, though that specific build cost about $1,407. So the tested Airias were slightly more expensive than the 404S, but they were 5mm deeper and dramatically lighter (also hooked).

That makes the 404S a reasonably priced option from a major brand, but the weight is hard to overlook when lighter and sometimes cheaper wheels are available at similar or lower prices. But the 404S does have one way it stands above its competition. It comes with a lifetime warranty that covers not just manufacturing defects but also damage from intended use. This will appeal to many riders who would rather have a dependable wheel than a slightly lighter one.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#8949. The Best Bike Lights for Triathletes in 2026, Tested and Reviewed

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Bottom Line: Each of the bike lights in our Best Bike Lights of 2026 list below has been tested on long rides by an experienced triathlete for many miles. Our reviewer is unbiased, with no brand relationships, meaning no brand has paid to appear in our list.

It’s that time of year again. You glance at your training plan, realize your post-work ride slot will now be taking place in the dark, and suddenly “bike light” jumps to the top of your shopping list. The good news is that bike lights in 2026 are significantly better than offerings from just a few years ago. You could even say they are light-years ahead (pun intended) of the bike lights from the 20th century. They are brighter, lighter, and – critically for triathletes – easier to mount on your bike than ever before.

But before you order the cheapest bike light on Amazon, there’s a bit more to think through. The cheapest option is far from the best, but you also don’t need to take out a second mortgage to buy a bike light either. Here’s what actually matters when buying lights as a triathlete, followed by the best options on the market right now.

As a light-toting triathlete, your goal isn’t just to see the road ahead of you; it is also to be seen. Public roads are far from perfectly safe, especially in today’s phone-addicted world filled with distracted drivers. But thankfully, having a bike light is one of the best ways to gain the attention of nearby drivers, reminding them to slow down and give you space as they pass by.

When shopping for a bike light, you want to consider two different design priorities, and pay close attention because most lights optimize for one or the other. First, you want a bike light that shines a powerful beam down the road, illuminating your path at speed in the dark. Second, you want a light that is designed to be seen. These lights use wide-angle optics, lateral emission, and attention-grabbing flash patterns to make you visible to cross-traffic and drivers approaching from the rear. Ideally, your bike light(s) do both.

For triathletes specifically, the lighting challenge runs deeper than a single unit on your bicycle. You might actually want three different lights for the corresponding sports. The ideal setup might include front and rear coverage on the bike, a headlamp or chest light for early-morning runs, and some form of visibility for open-water swims, especially those before sunrise. Each sport requires different hardware, but in this guide, we’ll focus on bike lights. Let’s help you figure out how to sort and sift through the hundreds of options on the market.

The standard brightness unit for sports lights is lumens. The higher the number, the brighter the light. But brighter isn’t always better. Some brands love to advertise max lumens at maximum output, but that can drain the battery in under two hours. Always check the light’s runtime at the mode you’ll actually use.

Consider the type of darkness you’ll be riding in, and how much light you’ll need. Not every triathlete will train in pitch darkness, so here is a quick reference of what you’ll find on the light market:

A pinpoint beam aimed straight ahead is great for one thing, and that’s seeing directly in front of you. But if you’re riding in the dark, you also want to have side visibility, not just from your own perspective, but for other riders and drivers to see you. The best bike lights have a wide spread beam that alerts drivers approaching from angles, not just head-on. Some lights now use multiple LEDs, which is worth considering if you ride in the dark year-round.

This is one of the most important aspects of a bike light because if the battery dies while you are riding in the dark 20 miles from home, you are SOL. Most bike lights are USB-C rechargeable, but runtime varies enormously. If you don’t get a light with a low-battery warning (ideally with several minutes of reserve before shutdown), make sure you keep tabs on how long you’ve been running it before it’s time to recharge.

This is where triathletes diverge from road cyclists. Aero bars, clip-on extensions, and non-standard cockpit shapes make standard clamp mounts useless in many setups. When shopping for lights, you’ll want to look for options that come with flexible silicone straps, GoPro-style mounts, or Garmin quarter-turn compatibility. Silicone straps cover the widest range of setups and are easy to transfer between bikes.

In the 2026 bike light market, there are a number of smart features that come with some of the more pristine options. Some of the features are just bells and whistles, but a few are genuinely helpful, especially for triathletes. Radar integration (Garmin Varia), ANT+ connectivity, automatic brightness adjustment, and brake-sensing technology are popular features that help improve function and safety on the bike. These are not marketing gimmicks – radar in particular can dramatically improve your confidence when riding on open roads with traffic.

Front light placement can be the trickiest part of lighting your tri bike. You can choose between below the basebar (the most aerodynamic option), midway down the aerobars (if the light rotates that direction), and arguably the best solution: adding a computer bridge to your aerobars and mounting the light on top or below it. Whatever you choose, test it on a bumpy road during daylight hours before relying on it in the dark. Remember that you’re not only looking for the light to stay attached, but also for the angle to remain stable as the light illuminates the road in front of you.

Rear lights are much more forgiving, with the seatpost being the most ideal spot for a rear-facing bike light. If you have limited seatpost access, you can mount a light on the seatstay. Just make sure your light is pointing backward rather than toward the sky or floor. If you have bottles or other gear mounted under or behind your seat, make sure they don’t block the bike light when they are fully loaded.

Output: 1,300 lumens front; 90 lumens rear

Battery life: 1.5 hrs front; 4.5 hrs rear

The Ion Pro and Flare bike lights do much more than illuminate through darkness. The paired set uses ANT+ to link the front and rear lights together, and you can control both from a compatible Garmin or Wahoo head unit. Up front, the Ion Pro has up to 1,300 lumens, which is more than enough for most low-light situations. It also has a clean beam pattern with solid front and side visibility, with a few hours of battery life across various power settings. In the rear, the Flare can be used with a 16-degree offset mount option that helps solve one of the most common triathlete problems: mounting a rear light on an angled seatpost or seatstay. The mount is sold separately, but it only costs $5.

Pros: ANT+ integration, offset rear mount solves tri-bike seatpost issues ($5 cost), strong front output Cons: Pricey for a set; front light only has 90 minutes of runtime at max output

Output: 130 to 1,000 lumens with six different modes

Battery life: 120 hrs on ECO FLASH; up to 2 hrs at max output

The Blinder has earned its spot on best-of lists for years, and the 2026 version is no exception. IP67 waterproofing and six different light modes make the Blinder 1000 suitable for a wide range of weather and light conditions, including midnight rain-riding. At low outputs, the Blinder 1000 lasts for days on a single charge. GoPro-style and standard handlebar mounts are both included, making it versatile on almost any tri cockpit.

Pros: Fully IP67 waterproof, versatile mounts, solid build quality, side window visibility

Cons: Heavier than some competitors at the same lumen output

Battery life: 1 hr at max output; up to 60 hrs at minimum output

If your friends call you “Nightrider,” then the AMPP 2200 might be the perfect bike light for you. With a max output of 2,200 lumens, the AMPP 2200 obliterates darkness in a way that can make you feel like you’re riding during the daytime. This is the light for those who ride in pitch darkness at speed, or those who live in extreme daylight climates such as Alaska or Iceland. While its top-end output is impressive, the AMPP 2200 includes different light modes that are ideal for riding in the dusk rather than the pitch black. At 500 to 800 lumens, the AMPP 2200 becomes a practical all-night light with sufficient battery reserve. Its included mount is quite secure, even on rough pavement. The trade-off is weight; at 211g, it’s the heaviest option on this list.

Pros: Exceptional max output, wide runtime range, secure mount, high-quality build

Cons: Heaviest light on this list; 2,200 lumens if overkill for those who don’t ride in complete darkness

Battery life: 4 to 80 hrs (front); 3 to 60 hrs (rear)

If you’re only looking for a pair of lights that will help you be seen, the Knog Frog combo could be the perfect fit. The front light output isn’t enough to illuminate a dark road, but not every triathlete wants to ride in the dark. Sometimes, you just want to be seen by drivers and cross-traffic, especially in low-light conditions. The combo’s battery life is fitting for the price point, and the pair is so light that you won’t even notice them. They come with a flexible silicone strap that wraps around virtually any tube shape, including aero bars. While they won’t light up a country road, the Knog Frog combo is great for being seen in the city, on the bike path, or on a foggy training loop.

Pros: Aero-bar compatible, extremely lightweight, very affordable, easy to use

Cons: 40 lumens won’t illuminate a dark road; not a standalone solution for night riding

Battery life: 16 hrs (day flash mode); 6 hrs (solid mode)

The Varia is a rear light that also functions as a vehicle radar. In terms of safety and security, it is one of the best bike lights on the market. When paired with a compatible Garmin head unit or Varia app, the light alerts you to vehicles approaching from behind, before you can even hear them. It is an incredibly useful safety feature, especially if you frequently ride in groups or on busy roads. If you get nervous riding on open roads, the Varia RTL515 could be the best option for you. While the light function itself isn’t anything special, the radar is the reason to buy it.

Pros: Vehicle radar is a game-changer on open roads; lightweight, impressive battery life, pairs with Garmin ecosystem

Cons: Expensive for a single rear light; radar requires a compatible head unit or phone mount

Battery life: 12 hrs constant; 30 hrs flash

In terms of bang for your buck, it’s hard to beat the Gravity Plus, which uses an accelerometer to detect braking and automatically increases brightness when you decelerate. It is effectively functioning as a brake light, and it is one of the cheapest options on this list. For triathletes who ride out of town, train with unpredictable stop-and-go conditions, or frequent group rides, the brake-sensing rear light is surprisingly effective. Runtime is excellent for a budget light, and you probably won’t even notice the added weight.

Pros: Brake-sensing technology, outstanding battery life, lightweight

Cons: 100 lumens is modest; a brighter light is necessary for riding in complete darkness

#8948. 7-Minute Yoga to Practice While Sitting at Your Desk

Yoga while sitting at your desk can be a simple way to soothe physical tension during the work day. This practice was created by instructor Laia Bové, who has taught students of all levels for more than a decade.

If you spend a lot of time hunched over your desk, you already know that it’s important to break the stagnation of long hours in front of your computer screen. But sometimes the time you think you’ll have to release the tension in your neck, shoulders, and upper back—likely before or after work—disappears due to other responsibilities, distractions, or just plain exhaustion.

This 7-minute yoga practice was made with the idea that you can sneak in a little yoga during work. These stretches target the most common areas where tension and aches arise when sitting at a desk and act as a quick reset. By the end of the seven minutes, you’ll feel a lot looser throughout your upper back and maybe even a little more ready to take on the rest of your day.

You can do this sequence between tasks, meetings, or calls, or after you power off your laptop and before you move on to other activities. You don’t need any special clothes or equipment—in fact, you don’t even need to get up from your chair.

Sit in your desk chair with your feet planted on the floor. Exhale and lower your chin toward your chest. Inhale and lift your chin toward the ceiling. Repeat that a few times.

Next time you exhale and lower your chin toward your chest, keep your chin lowered as you turn your head toward the right, as if you were drawing your nose toward your right shoulder. Take a breath here, then return to center with your chin still lowered. Then draw your nose toward your left shoulder. Return to center, then lift your chin to neutral.

Clasp your hands and rest them lightly behind your head. Point your elbows toward the sides of the room to prevent your hands from placing too much pressure on your head. Inhale as you lift your chest and draw your elbows slightly behind your chest, if possible, and slightly arch your back in a Cow Pose variation.

Keeping your hands where they are, exhale as you round your back, bring your elbows toward each other, and draw your navel toward your spine in a seated variation of Cat Pose. Repeat another round of this seated Cat-Cow variation.

Keeping your hands clasped behind your head, exhale as you lean toward the left, feeling a stretch along your right side. Inhale and return to center. Exhale as you bend toward the right, feeling a stretch along your left side. Inhale and return to center, then release your arms.

Place your fingertips on your shoulders and point your elbows toward the sides of the room. Draw your elbows toward each other in front of your chest as if you want them to touch, then lift them to point toward the ceiling, then point them toward the back wall, and then point them at the floor, moving in a large circular motion. Continue drawing elbow circles as many times as you like. Then switch directions.

Exhale and tilt your head toward the right, drawing your right ear toward your right shoulder. Inhale and return to center. Exhale and tilt your head toward the left, drawing your left ear toward your left shoulder. Repeat a few times.

Reach your arms out to your sides in a T shape, then cross your arms and wrap them around your chest as if you’re giving yourself a big hug. Take a few breaths here in Eagle Arms variation. Then repeat with the opposite arm on top. Release your arms.

With your arms relaxed at your sides, draw your shoulders up toward your ears and squeeze your muscles as tightly as you can—maybe you even scrunch the muscles in your face. Take a big breath in, then release your shoulders down and relax the muscles you were tightening. Repeat one more Shoulder Squeeze.

Take a big breath in through your nose and out through your mouth. Repeat as many times as needed until you’re ready to resume your day.

#8946. This $16 Tool Can Save You Thousands of Dollars Across the Life Span of Your Bike

Catch chain wear early and you could save hundreds—or more—on drivetrain replacements.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I’ve checked in thousands of bikes for service, and I used to hear this line all the time: “I ride the bike a lot, but it’s in great shape. The shifting just jumps around a little.” Once I would get to the step of putting a chain checker on the chain, that $16 tool might tell the story of hundreds of dollars in upcoming repairs.

A chain checker was one of my most recommended service tools to customers when I ran a bike shop service department. The key is to make sure you are buying the correct one and understand how to use it. The chain checker most shops I worked in was the Park Tool CC2 —the chain checker with the swivel dial.

This option was great because it gave customers and service advisors an easy visual on the wear level of a chain. But the biggest reason my favorite chain checker isn’t this one is because it does not give a clear reading on certain SRAM chains. Read on to find out which chain checker I suggest, why it can save you thousands of dollars across the life span of your bike, and how to use this small tool.

When a chain gets stretched it can cause issues like slow shifting, unexpected chain jumps, and the chain can have a slipping feeling under power. Sometimes these issues can also be mistaken for cable tension being off in a derailleur, but you can easily check the chain stretch at home if you have this chain checker.

It is extremely difficult to tell how worn a drivetrain is with the naked eye. By checking how worn a chain is, you can tell what other parts will need to be replaced. My favorite chain checker is the Pedro’s Chain Checker because it is compatible with most chain makes and models. It also retails for only $16 and it is small enough to fit in almost anyone’s tool roll or kit.

Many shops will recommend replacing an 11, 12, or 13 speed chain when a chain checker reads over 50 percent worn. If the chain is over 75 percent worn that recommendation changes to replacing a chain and cassette or freewheel (gears on the back wheel) and replacing chain, cassette or freewheel, and chainrings or crank (gears in the front near the pedals) when it measures over 100 percent worn. Typically 10-speed chains and lower have a bigger tolerance to stretch, with singlespeeds having the biggest acceptable stretch.

Many times a customer would ask if the shop could just throw a new chain onto a drivetrain that is past that 100 percent mark. If you do this, the shifting can actually get worse because the wear pattern in the new chain no longer lines up with the wear pattern on the existing cassette and chainrings. An even worse case scenario of putting a new chain on a worn drivetrain is chain suck. This is when a worn chainring can get stuck to the chain from the bottom of the pedal stroke. Then the chain gets sucked up and jammed between the chainring and the frame—possibly leading to damage on the frame. Once a drivetrain has a certain level of wear replacing only one part of the system does not work.

The price for some higher-end cassettes can range anywhere from $400 to $660 from brands like Shimano and SRAM. I go by a three-strike rule with chains (spokes too, but that’s a different story). For my own bikes I typically get three chains out of each cassette.

If you are on top of chain wear with a chain checker, this could save you almost $2,000 in cassette costs alone when using high-end SRAM cassettes. Remember, this price doesn’t include labor or the cost of chainrings—which you’ll need to replace if you keep running the chain until it’s above that 100 percent wear mark.

Some higher-end chainrings, like the SRAM Red direct-mount chainring, can run up to almost $300 per ring. If someone runs the whole drivetrain into the ground, then a checkup for shifting issues can quickly turn into a thousand-dollar bill on a high end drivetrain. If you’re running Shimano 105 or SRAM Rival, then being on top of chain wear might not save you thousands as quickly as running the highest end group set. Rest assured, overtime you’ll get there too. The better news is that Pedro's chain checker is so easy to use.

Start by dropping the tooth with the number one above it into the chain. Once the number one tooth is dropped in, then drop the tooth with the number two above it into the chain. Finally, try to drop the third tooth (numbered with a three) into the chain. If this tooth doesn’t drop in through the links in the chain, then good news! Your chain is less than 50 percent worn. If it drops halfway through the chain that means your chain is about 75 percent worn. Finally, if the tooth numbered three on the chain checker drops all the way through the chain that means it is between 75 percent and 100 percent worn. Typically I suggest if you have 11, 12, or 13 speed chains around that 50 percent worn mark change the chain soon to keep the rest drivetrain alive as long as possible.
