#8927. Want to Ride More at Home? These 9 Stationary Bikes Make Training Easy, Quiet, and More Consistent

Find the right at-home ride, whether you want a budget spin bike or a premium smart-bike setup.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Weather and daylight don’t always cooperate with our riding schedules. And when we add work hours, family time, yardwork, and life’s daily grind, finding time to ride can feel impossible. Especially during the dark days of late autumn and winter, indoor riding becomes the only realistic option for many of us.

Luckily, indoor cycling is no longer the boring, arduous task it was only a decade ago. Today’s stationary bikes range from no-frills machines to fully connected setups. Some even feature live and on-demand classes, immersive virtual rides, and easy syncing with popular fitness platforms like Strava.

All of our editors and test team ride or train indoors for at least part of the year, sometimes even during the summer months to escape the heat. We’ve logged countless hours on stationary bikes and standard indoor trainers. In our testing, we’ve wrestled with finicky machines, endured glitchy interfaces and endless updates, and spent plenty of time grinding out virtual miles from our basements, garages, and home gyms; some of our editors have even taught spin classes.

Stationary bikes come in three main styles: Upright, recumbent, and dual-action. Upright models feel most like riding a traditional outdoor bike. Recumbent bikes offer a more reclined position, while dual-action bikes add upper-body work to the pedaling action.

Our testing and reviews focus on upright stationary bikes made by cycling-specific brands and general fitness companies. To differentiate between the two, we call models from fitness companies “exercise bikes” and those from cycling brands “indoor bikes” in this story.

Exercise bikes by fitness-oriented brands often feature a more upright riding position, multi-position handlebars with foam padding, and wide, comfort-style seats. The pedals usually have toe clips for use with running shoes.

Indoor bikes from traditional cycling brands typically mimic the body position, ride feel, and functional layout of outdoor bikes and feature dropbars, brake hoods, adjustable crank length, and narrow saddles. They usually feature high resistance for sprint workouts and virtual racing. These bikes used to be expensive, but prices have dropped over the last three years, making them a great choice for everyday indoor riders (not only hardcore enthusiasts).

The BowFlex C6 has the most capability at a reasonable price. High-quality and adjustable, this bike features Bluetooth connectivity so you can connect to apps like Peloton, Zwift, and Schwinn Trainer to join community rides and track progress.

The monitor displays time ridden, speed, mileage, heart rate, and resistance level. It doesn’t show wattage or precise RPM (it displays them on a scale). However, it does measure them, and you can see that data if you connect it to third-party training apps.

The flywheel is smooth and heavy, and you can crank the resistance up significantly through 100 incremental levels via a knob. Toe cages let you ride the C6 in regular running shoes or flip the pedals over and clip in with Shimano SPD cleats.

A great feature is the unit’s silence—you can use it day or night without waking your family. It comes with a forearm heart rate monitor and a pair of 3-pound dumbbells for light upper-body workouts while riding.

Want a more immersive experience? Check out BowFlex’s Velocore. It features a 22-inch integrated console with tons of class and entertainment streaming options, and is compatible with Zwift, Peloton, and JRNY.

If you don’t like traditional exercise bikes and want something that closely replicates the fit and feel of riding your actual bike, the Zwift Ride is an ideal solution—and the recently updated V2 model addresses issues our editors experienced with the first-gen model by adding adjustable crank length and saddle setback.

At its core, the Ride is an indoor cycling setup that eliminates the hassle of constantly mounting and unmounting your bike from a trainer or dedicating one bike solely for indoor use. The frame is exceptionally sturdy and has proven itself time and again under the stress of multiple test riders’ workouts. Paired with the reliable Kickr Core 2 trainer—our Best Overall smart trainer pick—the setup delivers a premium ride experience.

However, the real magic lies in its seamless integration with Zwift’s virtual world. You can join races, group rides, guided workouts, or explore immersive digital landscapes alongside fellow “Zwifters.” The most popular virtual cycling platform globally, Zwift succeeds by stripping away the monotony of indoor training. It gamifies the experience while offering social and competitive features that you can engage with as much—or as little—as you like.

The Schwinn IC4 is ideal if you want quick, easy access to ride metrics; you can see your data on the display—no subscription necessary. It also has a stand for your phone or tablet, USB charging for your devices, water bottle holders, and weights so everything you need is at your fingertips.

If you’re in the mood to be pumped up by a live class, Rouvy, or Zwift race, the Bluetooth option lets you jump right into third-party apps. The bike comes with a free two-month subscription to Schwinn’s platform, JRNY, which offers workout programming tailored to your preferences and over 200 virtual courses.

If you like the concept of the Zwift Ride but want an indoor bike with more adjustability and refinement, Wahoo’s Kickr Bike Shift is one of the best options. It’s essentially a stripped-down version of Wahoo’s super-premium, $4,000 Kickr Bike Pro; the Shift doesn’t include the Pro’s motor-electromagnetic resistance, gradient simulation, and some finishing details. While nifty features, they’re overkill for almost every indoor rider.

Like the Kickr Bike Pro, the Shift is quiet, super smooth, and easily adjustable to fit multiple users in a household. It also features standard bicycle component attachment. This makes it easy to replicate your outdoor bike’s fit on the Kickr Shift with your favorite saddle and handlebar. If you want the convenience and silence of an indoor bike, and a premium indoor riding setup, the Shift is the one to get.

Peloton redefined at-home fitness with its original bike—a sturdy, low-maintenance machine built to withstand years of sweaty daily rides. Its true draw, though, has always been Peloton’s vast library of on-demand and live classes, now spanning not only cycling but also running, core, and boot camp sessions. With the Peloton app, you can even take workouts on the go.

For years, the bike itself saw few changes—until the Bike+ arrived. It keeps the durable frame and quiet belt drive but adds a redesigned handlebar and a larger 23.8-inch touchscreen that rotates 360 degrees, making it easy to follow floor-based workouts. The model also features forward-facing Sonos-tuned speakers and auto-resistance that adjusts automatically to match instructor cues. Not everyone will use it, but those who do will love the convenience.

The most notable update is Peloton IQ: a built-in camera that tracks your movements, offers real-time feedback, and counts reps. There’s even a small fan above the screen for added comfort.

However, these upgrades come at a premium: the Bike+ is significantly more than the standard Peloton Bike. If you want to save $1,000, the standard Bike features solid build quality and full access to Peloton’s unmatched training ecosystem. But it doesn’t include auto-resistance, high-quality speakers, a rotating screen, Peloton IQ, a phone tray, and a fan.

This budget-priced, belt-driven bike features a 35-pound flywheel and provides a smooth, quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable with a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches. Riders can also adjust the handlebar height and the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Although the Yosuda doesn’t connect to third-party sites, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned on the included single-button monitor. Below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame provides stability and durability, yet it’s easy to move thanks to the small wheels on the front edge.

If you’re spinning on a budget but want a connected experience, the Echelon EX-15 may be the stationary bike for you. This high-quality bike offers access to proprietary classes you can stream with an Echelon membership ($399.99 billed annually). Echelon’s membership isn’t limited to cycling content. The subscription offers rowing, running, strength training, yoga, and more. Enjoy workouts to music from artists including Pitbull and Lady Gaga—plus dance, EDM, hip hop, K-Pop, metal, Latin, and R&B.

The EX-15 bike itself is sized perfectly for smaller spaces, yet doesn’t skimp on comforts like an extra-large cushioned seat and padded handlebars. The mechanical knob lets you adjust resistance between 32 levels. You also get a free 30-day membership when you buy the EX-15 through Amazon.

It’s important to have one with solid construction and high weight capacity if you plan to put your stationary bike through the wringer. The Sunny Evolution Pro can withstand your most intense intervals and feels stable doing it. The 135-pound steel frame has a large footprint with leveling stabilizers in each corner to help prevent rocking.

Complementing that is a hefty 44-pound flywheel, which eliminates the inconsistent resistance you can feel near the top end of lighter wheels. The adjustable handlebar moves up and down and front to back, so you can dial in a position that's comfortable for your back, neck, and wrists.

The seat height accommodates riders with inseam lengths from 29 to 39 inches—a downside if you’re on the shorter side (Our 5-foot-2 barely made the cut, but awesome if you’re taller).

The Evolution Pro’s simplicity also makes it a great pick. Without Bluetooth connectivity (or even a monitor to display metrics), you can exercise without getting bogged down in numbers and be more in touch with your body at different PRE (perceived rate of exertion) levels.

The Keiser M3i is a studio-level spin bike with a clean, streamlined design and simplified interface. It has everything you need to nail your numbers in a hard workout, and then upload that data to apps like TrainingPeaks or Strava. The smooth flywheel is quiet, and its rear location means fewer sweat droplets land on it, so you can worry less about corrosion or wiping it down perfectly. The small monitor displays your power, cadence, time, gear, heart rate (if you’re wearing a connected strap), and total distance.

The media tray holds a phone or tablet above your handlebar so you can follow a route or guided workout as you ride, and it automatically uploads each effort in the included Keiser app to track your progress.

The saddle height adjustment uses preset stops; however, the wedge system lets you place the saddle in the precise spot you prefer. The looped handlebar is comfortable for a wide range of reaches, and the height adjustment accommodates riders as short as 4-foot-10 and as tall as 7 feet.

Stationary bikes come in three main options: upright, recumbent, and dual-action. The bikes recommended here are upright style, which puts you in a position that mimics how you’d sit on a traditional bicycle.

Recumbent exercise bikes seat you in a slightly reclined position with the pedals out in front of your hips rather than directly below, which can be easier on your back and neck. Dual-action exercise bikes have handlebars that move in and out, so riders incorporate their arms into the workout as they pedal.

Look for models with adjustable saddle height and position, plus adjustable handlebars. More adjustability makes it easier to find a comfortable riding position and get a good workout. Like a regular bicycle, a proper fit is crucial for the best experience. I like my indoor bike’s fit to match the position I ride outdoors.

All bikes feature bar-height adjustments, and some models let you adjust reach. Saddle height and setback adjustment options are also a must-have. They also have graduated markings, making it easier to get back to your preferred position after someone else uses the bike.

A dropbar offers hand positions that mimic road bikes, while a traditional bullhorn bar will be more familiar to those of you who frequent studio classes.

The two most common methods for regulating an indoor bike’s resistance are friction and magnets. Friction-based systems use leather or synthetic pads that press against a flywheel—It’s a simple, effective way to add precise, linear resistance. These resistance systems don’t require outside power to operate.

Magnetic resistance is quieter than friction systems. They use magnets (adjacent to the flywheel) to create an electric current that resists the wheel’s rotation. By increasing the current (strengthening the magnetic force), you have greater resistance. With no contact between the flywheel and magnets, this type of bike may offer a smoother ride than a friction-based one.

Some models use electromagnetic resistance controlled by software from a connected app. This allows platforms like Zwift to replicate hills and wind.

Bluetooth and ANT+ let you pair with training apps and sensors. If you use multiple apps, broad connectivity matters. Wi-Fi connectivity is nice to have if you plan to enter virtual races or use streaming-based setups.

Bluetooth-equipped exercise bikes let you transmit your ride data directly to third-party training apps like Peloton or Zwift for in-ride metrics. If it has ANT+ capability, you can connect to extra sensors—like a cadence tracker or heart rate monitor—and display that data on your monitor or tablet. It’s not totally necessary for an interactive experience.

If you want to join virtual classes but aren’t sure which you’ll like (or you enjoy several), look for a bike with connectivity and media compatibility that lets you join the most platforms.

Bluetooth and ANT+ let you pair with training apps and sensors. If you use multiple apps, broad connectivity matters. Wi-Fi connectivity is nice to have if you plan to enter virtual races or use streaming-based setups.

Most indoor bikes function similarly; the accessories that set them apart. The most basic models are as simple as it gets, just an ergometer with a weighted flywheel and a pad to set resistance. At the other end of the spectrum are bikes like the Peloton, with elaborate software for recorded and live classes.

Decide how much technology you actually need for your indoor rides. Some cyclists want a feature-rich experience with training plans, classes, and group rides, while others want a stripped-down bike that covers the bare essentials.

Measure your available space before buying. If you will need to move it, also check the model’s weight and whether it has wheels.

Seat comfort matters; if possible, test-ride the seat that comes with your stationary bike before buying to make sure it's comfortable for you. Most stationary bikes come with a basic, comfort-style saddle. Models that allow you to swap the seat for aftermarket options offer more flexibility.

Seat comfort matters. Most stationary bikes come with a basic, comfort-style saddle. Models that allow you to swap the seat for aftermarket options offer more flexibility.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8925. Garmin’s New Screen-Free Fitness Band Takes Aim at WHOOP and Oura With No Subscription Required

The CIRQA band tracks a broad sweep of daily health and fitness metrics, giving Garmin users a fuller view of life on and off the bike.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Most fitness trackers come with a second price tag: a monthly fee for seeing the data they collect. Garmin’s $200 CIRQA Smart Band needs no subscription for core health, sleep, and activity tracking. That sets it apart from WHOOP’s and Oura’s paid membership models. Garmin’s pitch is straightforward: buy the band, wear it around the clock, and check the data in Garmin Connect without another recurring bill. It’s a refreshing proposition in a world lousy with subscriptions.

Very basically, the CIRQA is a screen-free fabric band designed for all-day wear on the wrist or upper arm; the concept is similar to the Whoop band. It tracks heart rate, sleep, HRV, stress, skin temperature, Pulse Ox, and Garmin’s Body Battery estimate. Garmin claims up to 10 days of battery life. The band supports more than 80 activity types, uses your phone for GPS, and can broadcast heart rate to a cycling computer. Garmin pitches the lack of a screen as a feature for riders who want the data but don’t want to wear a smartwatch.

The single button handles one favorite activity, which you set in Garmin Connect. Press it once to start recording and again to stop; the band vibrates and flashes an LED to confirm. You can start other activities in the app, and CIRQA can automatically detect some sessions from movement and exertion data. That keeps the band clean and simple, with setup and seeing the details handled through the phone.

I’ve tracked rides with cycling computers since the days of the fabled Garmin Edge 500. Over the years, I’ve sent those files through Strava, TrainingPeaks, and a rotating cast of other platforms. Plenty of them can tell me what I did on the bike. Garmin’s appeal, and maybe its best selling point, is the Garmin Connect app.

With a Garmin cycling computer, your ride data already lives in Garmin Connect. Add the CIRQA, or another Garmin wearable, and the app puts that training alongside sleep, stress, HRV, and other health metrics. The CIRQA’s unique appeal isn’t any one metric the band collects. It’s that those metrics feed into the same ecosystem as your ride data, giving you a more complete picture of your training in the full context of your day.

That can be useful if you’re trying to make better training decisions yourself, or if you work with a coach who wants more context than your power files and weekly mileage can provide. A hard workout looks different after a great night’s sleep than it does after a week of poor sleep and high stress. Putting that data in one place makes it easier to see when a planned session fits or when it's time to adjust the plan.

Wearable device options are more plentiful than ever, and the CIRQA won’t be the right pick for everyone. Its clearest audience is the rider who already uses Garmin Connect and wants health and recovery data alongside cycling workouts. If your bike computer already uploads rides there, the CIRQA adds context about what happens between them. That connection is the main reason to choose it.

It should also appeal to people who want to track sleep, stress, and activity without taking on another subscription. You don’t need a paid membership for CIRQA’s core tracking, which makes it a good option for riders who want to monitor their daily data without another recurring bill.

The other clear fit is someone who wants less screen time on their wrist. The CIRQA has no display or smartwatch notifications. Maybe you wear an analog watch and want to keep it that way; maybe you’re tired of your smartwatch and want a wearable that quietly collects data for you to check later. If you want live metrics and notifications or even the time at a glance, the CIRQA probably isn’t for you.

Sleep tracking and HRV status worked seamlessly for me. I don’t find much value in comparing one wearable’s numbers directly with another’s. It’s more important for the numbers to be consistent and CIRQA’s were. Its readings tracked with how I felt from one day to the next, and also mirrored the trend lines of numbers from other smartwatches I’ve been testing, which made them useful as context rather than scores I had to chase.

Having sleep, HRV, and stress inside Garmin Connect alongside my ride data made those numbers actionable for me. I’m self-coached, so I’m deciding every day whether to do the workout on my calendar, go easier, or take a day off. Garmin Connect’s ability to bring my on-bike training and the rest of my day together in one place felt like the most useful thing about the CIRQA band.

The band has a single button, an underrated feature, and maybe a Band-Aid, too. I liked being able to start and stop an activity manually instead of hoping the band’s auto-detection caught it, especially for commutes, hikes, and runs. In general, auto-detection did a good job with walks, runs, hikes, gym workouts, and swims. My twice-a-day e-bike daycare trip was a different story: CIRQA picked it up about half the time. If it were more consistent on those rides, the button would matter less. But even if automatic activity tracking worked perfectly, having a manual stop/start button feels useful.

As someone trying to avoid another subscription, I see CIRQA as Garmin’s best alternative to WHOOP. There’s meaningful overlap in the day-to-day metrics, like sleep and HRV. WHOOP packages those metrics more neatly into an easy-to-read Strain/Recovery dashboard. CIRQA’s advantage is the Garmin Connect app, which combines ride data with all the metrics CIRQA tracks, which makes it an easy sell for existing Garmin users. But its lack of a subscription makes it easy to recommend to everyone else looking for a wearable device.

#8922. Locust Pose Might Be a Simple Backbend, But It Can Help Improve Your Posture

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about the backbend Locust Pose first appeared in the July-August 1996 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

If a picture is worth a thousand words, then our posture speaks volumes. Poor carriage of the torso—rounded shoulders, sunken chest, and a downward cast of the eyes—generally suggests a negative state of being. Good posture, on the other hand—shoulders rolled back and down, chest lifted, and an energetic carriage—demonstrates confidence and a sense of purpose.

All the backbending yoga postures help create this physical expression of assurance. You feel better, have more energy, and benefit from an enhanced respiratory system. The internal alignment of the organs is refined as we adjust and improve the external alignment.

The postures actually have the potential to positively and profoundly affect you on all levels: physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual. Approaching your asanas with this awareness is the key to the enrichment of your practice.

The repertoire of backbending postures, or hyperextensions of the spine, is vast. In this article, we are going to focus on one of the more basic back-bending poses, Grasshopper or Locust Pose (Salabhasana). There are several variations of this posture, according to different systems or styles of hatha yoga. We will practice two versions of Locust, beginning with Salabhasana One as described in B.K.S. Iyengar’s Light on Yoga.

Locust is excellent for correcting poor posture, as well as for counteracting the development of kyphosis, the rounding of the upper back. It tones the whole posterior of the body, strengthens the abdominals, and enhances digestion.

Begin by lying face down on your mat, with your arms at your sides near your hips, palms facing upward. Tuck your chin in, forehead on the floor.

Engage your abdominals by drawing your navel in and up, to stabilize your lower back. Contract your buttocks and quadriceps. Keep the knees, legs, and feet together. Exhale the breath as you simultaneously raise the head, chest, arms, and legs. Look forward and up. Hold and breathe for five to 10 seconds. Keep the abdominals firm so you feel the support from underneath.

Exhale as you come out of the pose, returning to base position. Turn your head to the side and completely relax. Repeat once or twice more.

Full Locust begins in the same base position, but with the arms outstretched at shoulder level, perpendicular to the body. The palms are facing down, and the chin is on the mat. The knees, legs, and feet are together.

Engage your abdominal muscles by drawing your navel in and up; contract your buttocks and quadriceps. This time, inhale the breath as you raise the arms, chest, head, and legs. Look forward and up. Breathe naturally as you hold the posture for five to 10 seconds. Keep your shoulders away from your earlobes as you continue to stretch your arms back and slightly upward. Palms remain facing the floor. The idea is to lift the entire body upward as you balance on the center of your abdomen.

Exhale as you come out of the pose, returning to base position, and relax. Repeat once or twice more.

If your lower back is sensitive or you are prone to chronic neck tension, you may want to practice the pose in the following stages.

Lie on your stomach, face down, arms at your sides near your hips. Palms are facing up, the chin is tucked in, and the forehead is on the floor. Legs are hip-distance apart. Firm the buttocks and abdominals as well as the quadriceps.

Inhale the breath. Exhaling, raise just the arms to about hip level, keeping the palms facing up. The head remains on the floor. Lengthen the neck and focus on strengthening your back muscles. Feel your shoulder blades pull down your back and slightly together.

Keep the abdominals, buttocks, and legs firm. Exhale and lower down.

Next, repeat what you’ve just done and add the lifting of the chest. The neck and head will come up as well, but keep looking downward so the neck remains extended rather than arched. Inhale in your base position. Exhale and raise the arms only. Inhale and hold. Ex-haling, raise the chest. Again, hold and breathe rhythmically for five to 10 seconds. Exhale as you lower down.

In the same beginning position, inhale the breath, and exhale raising the arms up. Hold and inhale. Exhale, raising the chest. Hold and inhale. Finally, exhale and raise the legs. Hold and breathe. Keep looking at the floor, focusing on lengthening the body from the top of your head to your fingertips on down to your toes. When you’re ready, lower down on an exhalation. Turn your head to the side, release the pose completely, and relax.

A natural inclination after performing a back bend is to pull your knees to your chest. So after your last repetition, you may want to got into Child’s Pose: Kneel back onto your heels, folding your torso over your thighs with your head resting on the floor in front of your knees. Arms are at your sides with palms facing up.

If your head doesn’t rest on the floor easily, simply fold your arms underneath your forehead for support.

#8921. Are High-Intensity Workouts Messing With Your Cortisol?

If you’ve scrolled through social media lately, you’ve probably seen wellness influencers claim high-intensity exercise increases cortisol, the infamous “stress hormone” that, in excess amounts, can lead to fatigue, weight gain, trouble sleeping, high blood pressure, and elevated blood sugar.

Many influencers say to switch to a no-stress, low-sweat regimen. And while low-intensity exercises such as Pilates, treadmill walking, or yoga are valid ways to work out—and serve as excellent cross-training activities for runners—HIIT workouts (like hill repeats, sprint intervals, and tempo runs) are key if you’re training for a race or looking to build speed and power.

But are high-intensity runs actually messing with your hormones, or is the wellness side of the internet spreading misinformation? We’re here to separate fact from fiction.

Cortisol is a hormone made by your adrenal glands, which are located on top of your kidneys and are part of your body’s endocrine system.

“Cortisol helps regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and the immune response, and it makes energy available when the body is under stress—including during exercise,” says Dr. Aysegul Eren, M.D., endocrinologist and medical director of the Adrenal Program at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

This hormone rises when your body faces increased physical or metabolic demand, such as exercise, illness, fasting, low blood sugar, or psychological stress, Eren explains. During exercise, cortisol naturally spikes as a way to provide energy to your body so it can perform. Viewed through that lens, cortisol is an important part of your body’s response to exercise and your ability to complete workouts.

“Higher-intensity exercise reliably causes a temporary cortisol rise, generally related to exercise intensity,” Eren says. “This is normal physiology, not something harmful to prevent.”

How long cortisol remains elevated depends on the stressor, according to Dr. Feyza Erenler, M.D., an endocrinologist at Tufts Medical Center. It may be minutes to hours for a brief stimulus like exercise, she explains.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 studies on HIIT, published in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, found that cortisol increased immediately after exercise, often fell below baseline about two hours later, and returned to baseline within 24 hours.

“There’s no evidence that a specific number of HIIT sessions causes chronically high cortisol,” Eren says. “The more relevant concern is overtraining—chronic training without adequate recovery—which can lead to persistent underperformance. ‘Too much’ is individual, depending on training load, sleep, nutrition, recovery, and other stressors.”

In fact, research shows physical activity can actually lead to lower cortisol levels. A 2026 study in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that those who did 150 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise (50 to 85% of their max heart rate) every week for a year saw a reduction in long-term cortisol levels.

Symptoms frequently attributed to “high cortisol,” such as fatigue, poor sleep, anxiety, or difficulty losing weight, don’t indicate that a person has high cortisol, according to Erenler. “These symptoms are extremely common and nonspecific and can occur for many different reasons,” she says.

Signs of true high cortisol—not the brief, self-resolving spike during exercise—include bruising, muscle weakness (particularly in the upper legs), wide purple stretch marks, worsening high blood pressure or diabetes, and sometimes changes in fat distribution, according to Eren.

If you’re experiencing any of the above symptoms, Eren recommends discussing them with your healthcare provider rather than trying to diagnose yourself with high cortisol all on your own (or with the help of a chatbot). Chronic high cortisol levels that are undiagnosed can cause high blood pressure, diabetes, muscle and bone loss, higher infection risk, and cardiovascular complications.

But rest assured, cortisol disorders are rare. For instance, Cushing syndrome, a condition where you have too much cortisol in your blood for a long period of time, only affects 10 to 15 people per million each year, according to the Endocrine Society. Cushing syndrome is caused by a tumor on the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, not too much high-intensity exercise.

“During exercise, cortisol temporarily rises in response to the physiological stress and then decreases as the body recovers and the stressor resolves,” Erenler says. “In Cushing syndrome, cortisol exposure remains inappropriately elevated over time, and the normal regulatory mechanisms—including the normal circadian pattern and suppression of cortisol production—are disrupted.”

For most healthy people, there’s no need to try to suppress the normal cortisol response to exercise. Instead, the goal should be a sustainable training program that includes adequate recovery, sufficient sleep and nutrition, and variation in workout intensity.

“Don’t worry about the temporary rise in cortisol that occurs with exercise,” Eren says. “It’s a normal part of the body’s response to physical activity, not a sign that exercise is harming you.”

Erenler agrees and says the goal isn’t to eliminate cortisol—it’s to challenge your body appropriately and give it enough recovery to adapt to the stress you’re placing on it.

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

One of the highest cents-per-mile redemptions in all of travel rewards

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

This detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.

Here's what makes it moderate rather than easy — and how to handle each challenge. ### Challenge 1: Finding Available Award Space ANA business class partner award seats are genuinely scarce. ANA doesn't release large blocks of partner availability, and what they do release on prime routes like JFK–NRT goes quickly. This is the single biggest obstacle. **The fix:** Search at exactly 331 days out, use United.com for the most accurate availability search, and have flexibility in your travel dates by at least one week in either direction. ### Challenge 2: The Multi-Program Booking Process You're searching on one airline's website (United), transferring points from a bank program (Chase/Amex) to a third airline's loyalty program (Virgin Atlantic), and then booking through that third airline's portal. It's a three-step process across three platforms. **The fix:** Follow the step-by-step process above methodically. Don't rush. Confirm availability before touching your points. ### Challenge 3: Points Accumulation 90,000 miles is a meaningful balance — but it's achievable. Chase Sapphire Reserve's welcome bonus alone can get you most of the way there. This earns a 4 out of 5 on the "Easy to Earn" scale for good reason. ### The Bottom Line If you've successfully transferred points and booked an award before, you can do this. The learning curve is real but short. The reward — flying ANA "The Room" over the Pacific for $60 in fees — makes every minute of research worthwhile.

Yes, but it requires 180,000 miles total. Many experienced travelers book one-way in business class using miles and return in economy on a paid ticket or use a different program for the return flight. This stretches your points further.

No. When booking ANA-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic, there are no fuel surcharges. You will pay taxes and fees of approximately $50-$150 depending on the route. This is a significant advantage over booking through some other partner programs.

This is the primary risk. Award seats can be taken by other travelers while you are in the process of transferring points. The mitigation strategy is to only search and transfer during off-peak hours, and to use programs with instant transfer speeds like Chase and Amex.

ANA "The Room" booked through Virgin Atlantic miles is one of the single highest-value redemptions in travel rewards. Ninety thousand miles gets you a private suite on a transpacific flight that costs $5,000-$8,000 in cash. The booking process requires patience and planning, particularly around the 331-day availability window, but the payoff is a genuinely world-class travel experience. If Japan is on your bucket list and you have been building transferable points, this is the redemption to target.

#8916. Cold, Dark, Rainy? The 10 Best Editor-Tested Indoor Bike Trainers Keep Your Training on Track

Our editors tested the best indoor bike trainers for winter miles, Zwift rides, and every budget.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Well, friends, it’s that time of year again. Colder temperatures and shorter daylight hours mean indoor riding season is right around the corner for many of us—if it hasn’t already arrived where you live. But thankfully, newer trainer tech and digital connectivity make those boring nights spent staring at your basement wall or garage door while endlessly spinning the pedals a thing of the past.

Smart trainers—some priced under $500—connect to Zwift and Rouvy, popular platforms that feature virtual worlds, group rides, and even organized races. Plus, lower prices on nicely-equipped indoor bikes mean you no longer have to wrestle with putting your bike on the trainer or ruining pricey components with sweat.

Our editors test trainers year-round, from budget-friendly units to the most advanced smart bike models currently available. We do workouts and ride a ton of base miles; some staff even compete at a high level in virtual racing leagues, giving us important feedback on trainer accuracy, stability, and durability.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is our Best Overall Indoor Trainer because it’s the perfect choice for most riders. It combines Wahoo’s excellent base-model direct-drive trainer with Zwift’s singlespeed cog and virtual shifting. The system sets up easily and works with almost any bike, regardless of gear range or number of speeds. (You can easily swap the Zwift Cog with a cassette if you don’t like the virtual gearing.) This enables multiple riders in a household to share one trainer, even if their bikes have different drivetrains or gearing.

I used the first-generation Kickr Core as my home setup for four years without any issues. Wahoo’s recent updates to the Core only make an already great smart trainer even better. Test Editor Dan Chabanov recently used the new Kickr Core 2 for three months after switching from the more expensive Kickr V6. He said, “Honestly, I can’t say I’ve noticed any kind of downgrade.”

On paper, the Kickr Core 2 has lower maximum wattage, less grade simulation, and slightly less claimed accuracy. In practice, the ride feel is almost identical on both models. Like the Kickr V6, the Core now features Wi-Fi (along with Bluetooth and ANT+) for smooth connectivity and faster data transmission for online events. “Truly, the only reason to opt for the pricier V6 is that it folds slightly smaller and is easier to move around,” Chabanov concluded.

The Zwift Cog uses virtual shifting to change gears instead of your bike’s shifters and derailleurs. Unfortunately, virtual shifting only works in Zwift. If you plan to ride without Zwift (or on another platform), purchase the Kickr Core 2 with a cassette.

Tired of putting your bike on the trainer every time you want to ride indoors?

Dedicated training bikes, such as the Zwift Ride, are a great option for indoor riding. This way, you have a bike on the trainer that’s always ready to ride. No more fumbling to remove your wheel or wearing down tires. The Ride’s adjustment range also makes it easy to set up and share with multiple riders in a household.

“After more than a year of heavy use by my wife and me, the Zwift Ride has proven to be a durable, impressively quiet alternative to abusing our 'good' bikes on a trainer, with excellent Zwift integration and easy adjustability for our multi-rider household,” said Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips.

Zwift’s recent updates addressed our criticisms of the original Ride. The V2 now fits more riders (4’10” to 6’6”), adds saddle adjustability, and increases the bar diameter. It also includes Zwift’s multi-position crank with lengths from 160mm to 175mm, which used to be a $100 upcharge.

If you ride indoors and want a dedicated setup that integrates with Zwift out of the box (and don’t want to spend thousands of dollars for a premium indoor bike), the Zwift Ride is an excellent option. Zwift sells the Ride Smart Frame alone (without a trainer) for $800 if you already have a direct-drive trainer.

Since launching in 2012, the Wahoo Kickr has consistently been one of the best indoor trainers and a favorite of Bicycling’s staff. While the sixth version of the venerable smart trainer is more of an update than a wholesale redesign, the changes help the Kickr rank ahead of other high-performance smart trainers.

The latest iteration features the same flywheel as the previous one, so the two units look virtually identical. As a result, both generations experience the same ride feel. The Kickr ramps up smoothly and correctly as you accelerate. Power accuracy is very good, and most riders will find the claimed 1-percent accuracy to be true.

Despite its high price and lack of cassette-sizing options, the latest Kickr is a solid choice. It’s the best option for performance-minded cyclists who push big watts or racers who require accuracy and improved connectivity for online events.

If you need a basic, budget-friendly trainer that gets the job done in a pinch—and offers compatibility with third-party apps like Zwift—the Tacx Boost Trainer Bundle is a solid option. With its magnetic roller, you can manually adjust resistance across ten levels. And because the Boost uses magnetic resistance instead of fluid or fans, it stays relatively quiet. The loudest sounds you’ll hear are your drivetrain and the tire on the roller.

The bundle includes a Garmin speed sensor and a front wheel block to keep your bike level while riding. It also folds up easily for compact storage. For an easy-to-use, low-cost, no-frills setup, this one covers the essentials.

The Saris Fluid2 is a good trainer at a reasonable price. This makes it a solid pick for riders who need something basic to keep up with their training plan on rainy days, rehab from injury, or get back into riding before heading outside onto the bike path, road, or trails.

The Fluid2’s wheel-on design means you don’t need to fumble with your drivetrain to set it up, and the fluid resistance provides a smooth, progressive ride feel. Although this version isn’t compatible with Zwift, Rouvy, or other online platforms, the Saris combo kit (for $40 more) includes a wheel sensor that adds connectivity. Also be sure to get an adaptor kit if your bike has a thru axle rear wheel.

Instead of buying that no-name $50 or $80 trainer, spend a little more for a proven trainer from a trusted brand. While it looks similar to Saris’ Fluid 2 (above), the Mag Plus uses a magnetic sensor to provide resistance instead of fluid. This saves a little money and gives you a linear feel (versus the Fluid’s progressive resistance). However, a big downside is that they tend to wear out tires pretty quickly, especially pricey, high-performance rubber.

Mag trainers have been around for decades (I’ve had several from different brands over the years); the tech hasn’t changed much and they don’t have any smart features. If you plan to ride Zwift or Rouvy, you need to install a wheel sensor. If you need a super basic trainer that gets the job done for only $100, the Mag Plus is your best bet.

The Neo 3M matches the Wahoo Kickr in power measurement (up to 2,200 watts with 1% accuracy) and maximum simulated gradient (up to 25%), but it has two unique features. The Neo generates its own electricity, so you can use it without external power (though it works best when plugged in). And, like an old-school Nintendo Rumble Pack, the Neo 3M vibrates to simulate a wide range of road surfaces—from gravel to cobblestones to concrete slab roads—when you’re riding Zwift.

Unlike other direct-drive trainers that use belts or rollers to transmit power, the Neo 3M uses a metal flywheel with magnets that interact with electrical coils to moderate resistance. Combined with the built-in motion plates, the trainer has an impressively realistic ride feel. However, the Neo 3M lacks a native high-speed data transfer mode or built-in Wi-Fi—a great feature for competitive virtual racing—but Garmin offers a separate adaptor.

The Wahoo Kickr Bike Pro is the indoor trainer of choice for riders seeking the best possible experience—and who have the space for a dedicated setup. At $4,000, it’s like investing in an extra bike that you can’t even ride outside. However, for many riders, the price is worth it since it’s always ready to go. You don’t need to install a bike or connect any devices. Plus, highly corrosive sweat and salt from trainer rides won’t damage your outside bike.

The Kickr Bike Pro adjusts to almost all bike fit measurements. Or, if you had a Guru, Retül, or Trek bike fit, you can plug the dimensions into the Wahoo app for more precise setup. Since the Bike uses virtual shifting, you can program it to any Shimano, SRAM, or Campagnolo drivetrain you want to ride. You can select the gear ratios and the number of teeth per cog.

The Kickr Bike Pro’s incredible ride feel comes from its high-tech flywheel with motor; it adds resistance while simulating the inertia of real-world riding. The Pro provides a coasting feel along with realistic braking and shifting. The system also features a piston-like mechanism that reflects virtual elevation changes by adjusting the angle between the bike and the ground (up to 20% incline and 15% decline).

If the Kickr Bike Pro’s $4,000 price tag is a little out of reach, check out the Kickr Bike Shift. It’s similar to the Pro in adjustment, but ditched the fancy flywheel and gradient-change feature—and it saves you almost $1,500.

Feedback’s Omnium Over-Drive is compact, lightweight (14 pounds), and sets up and breaks down fast. That’s why these portable trainers are ubiquitous in parking lots and team tents at bike races. These same traits also make it a great option for riders with small apartments or training while away from home.

However, this portable trainer isn’t light on features. Two 4-inch magnetic drums provide progressive resistance up to 1,050 watts (at 55 mph). Thanks to its height-adjustable fork mount and sliding base, the Over-Drive accommodates most bikes, wheel sizes, and quick-release or thru-axle configurations. Feedback includes a durable tote bag for storage under a bed, in your garage, or in a car trunk.

The trainer’s compact size makes it easy to carry on a plane as checked luggage (or in your bike bag)—I brought it along many times on trips to Asia and Europe. Plus, the Omnium’s quiet ride won’t disturb neighbors in a hotel room.

Wahoo’s unique-looking Kickr Rollr is a novel approach to indoor trainers. It’s a great option for those who need to install or remove their bike quickly. This makes it easy to use in a pinch, such as when an afternoon thunderstorm rolls in and threatens to cancel your training ride.

At the front, the Rollr features an A-shaped bracket that holds your bike’s front wheel with a tool-free clamp that accommodates tires up to 2.1 inches/53mm wide. At the back, the Rollr’s two drums cradle your bike’s rear tire, and an external flywheel adds resistance.

This design makes it quick and easy to put a bike on the Kickr Rollr, swap out multiple bikes, or share a trainer with other riders. However, we don’t recommend this trainer for riders who do a lot of out-of-the-saddle, high-intensity training or for users who regularly race on Zwift. (A direct-drive trainer will be better suited for these tasks.)

While the Rollr is adjustable for different wheelbases, the adjustment is limited and optimized for road bikes. This means long-wheelbase mountain bikes might not fit (most road or gravel bikes shouldn’t have any issues). Since the trainer doesn’t read power, you must have a power meter to use the Rollr’s smart features.

Direct-drivetrainers attach to your bike’s rear dropouts and replace your rear wheel with a resistance unit. These trainers are typically quieter than other systems, provide more accurate power readings, and are ideal for high-power efforts.

Friction trainers use a roller pressed against your bike’s rear tire. They’re lighter, (usually) more affordable, and more portable than other systems. However, friction trainers can be very noisy and wear out tires.

Rollers are a time-tested indoor riding platform. They use three drums (rollers) that you ride on, so they require balance. While some rollers have resistance, many don’t.

Smart bikes are dedicated indoor training bikes. These trainers are heavy and take up space, but they’re a great option if you have a bigger budget, are tired of taking your bike on/off the trainer, or don’t want to wreck your outdoor bike with sweat and salt.

Typically, a smart trainer is an indoor trainer that can wirelessly communicate power data with a training app on a smartphone or computer. Most smart trainers also work with virtual riding platforms like Zwift by automatically adjusting resistance to simulate changes in terrain.

The popularity of online riding platforms means most newer trainers are “smart” and will both transmit your data and adjust resistance. These features often add to the cost of a new trainer. But prices are falling; you can find connected trainers—such as the Saris M2—for less than $200.

If you want to try Zwift but don’t have a smart trainer, you can still log virtual miles using a Bluetooth speed sensor. Check out our guide to getting started here.

Compatibility: With axle attachment standards and widths frequently changing, check if the trainer you want offers different attachment options (such as thru-axle adaptors, or for direct-attachment trainers, free-hub options). Some trainers come with them. If yours doesn’t, you’ll need to purchase them separately. The Robert Axle Project is my go-to resource for replacement thru-axles and adapters.

Noise: While most manufacturers can get away with using words like “silent” and “virtually silent” to describe the noise level of their trainers, there are other factors to consider, such as the sound your bike’s drivetrain makes as you pedal, and if you use one, the fan that’s whirring away to keep you cool and simulate wind speeds. To get a better idea of how loud “silent” actually is, we used a decibel meter to record the noise levels of each trainer being ridden at 15 and 25 mph. Decibels ranged from 68 (comparable to a vacuum cleaner) to 85 (a diesel truck going 40 mph); the fan alone measured 71. To get an idea of how significant a seemingly minor jump in decibels can be, 70 is twice as loud as 60, and 80 is twice as loud as 70.‌

Stability: Trainer crashes are rare, but not unheard of when you’re going cross-eyed trying to beat your PR on a workout. Typically, the wider the trainer’s base, the more stable it will be. Many have a leveling feature for uneven surfaces.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8914. How Yoga Brings You Closer to Yourself and the Life You Want

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about yoga as a science and an art first appeared in the January-February 1977 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Yoga is a science, an art, and a technique which spans the multilevel functioning of the individual. It is a science because of its empirical approach, presented most completely by the classic Yoga Sutras of Patanjali at least 1,000 years ago. Science is defined as a methodology which requires empirical proof of its theories; it requires that which proves a theory be easily repeatable by another experimenter if he/she follows the rules of the experiment.

Yoga, by this definition, is indeed a science. Its rules are given in sutra form and the presentation of Patanjali is a “how-to” book of the highest order. The practitioner need only follow the lead of Patanjali in order to have his own personal empirical results. (It is true that the directions are in parts esoteric and apparently illusive; this points out the necessity of having a teacher upon whom the practioner can rely for advice during certain intervals.) In addition to the work by Patanjali, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika and the Gheranda and Shiva Samhita are references which can explain the science of yoga.

But yoga is an art, too. Individuals have dedicated their lives to the perfection of this art. This does not necessarily imply the production of tangible output such as texts, although these have been produced in the history of traditional Indian thought. Rather, the use of the word “art” in this context implies the movement toward perfection within, the embodiment of beauty as it can be expressed through the human being. If one dedicates his/her life to the art of yoga, this implies a dedication which does not involve merely daily practice numbering a few hours. Instead, it implies a minute by minute practice which spans years, and some believe, lifetimes of existence.

The art of yoga is the practice of yoga on all levels of existence; this means every thought, action, dream, relationship, food intake, sexual activity, occupation, etc., are brought into the wider perspective of observation in light of the individual’s desire to understand the Self. This understanding does not imply intellectual understanding alone. It implies the “living” or the “being” in the Self rather than just mentally knowing about the Self. One can compare this to the experience of being in a hurricane with merely reading about the experience of a hurricane; the effect would be quite different.

One who lives in the Self has come into a wholeness of being, possibly for us all by virtue of our human existence, but available presently to only a handful due a complex interplay of events which, for whatever reasons, has brought them to a newer threshold of consciousness. Thus the art of yoga lies in bringing perfection into action through becoming one with oneself.

Part of the ability to do this lies with the powerful psychological technique of “acting as if.” If one wishes to meditate, one often begins by acting as if one were meditating. As the form of meditation is assumed, the content of meditation begins to be experienced. If one acts as if one loves another, and acts with sincerity and with honesty, often feelings of love toward that person do begin to flow. So with yoga. If one watches and practices as if yoga were an art and the Self were the artist, then this lends validity to the possibility of this being true.

This brings one to the question of technique. Yoga is also a concrete way of bringing about profound physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual changes within the individual. The student is instructed in yama and niyama (basic ethical precepts), in asanas (meditative postures), in pranayama (conscious voluntary control of the energy associated with breath), in pratyhara and dharana (watching and observing the mind), and finally, in dhyana, or meditation. The final experiencing of samadhi (union) cannot be taught; it is both the result of the foregoing disciplines and independent of them. The understanding of this apparent paradox is part of the process of learning about yoga.

Thus yoga can be seen from the angles of science, art or technique. It can be approached as a small practice of one’s life, or as the way that life is lived, a quality which is brought to live which liberates one from the strong bonds of ego.

#8913. Replacing Your Bike Chain Is Easier Than You Think—Here’s How to Do It at Home

A step-by-step home repair guide to measuring, removing, and installing a bike chain.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Replacing a chain is a great way for someone to tap into their home bike maintenance potential. It’s a pretty straightforward process once you’re used to it, especially if you have the existing chain to measure from. I typically recommend being familiar with a few skills before diving into replacing your chain. The first skill to know is adjusting your front and rear derailleurs. The second is knowing how to use a chain checker. The third is being familiar with a pre bike check. This last one is especially helpful because it will allow you to run through the bike to see if there are any other issues before diving into swapping out your chain. Again, these skills are not required skills to replace a chain, but having some familiarity with the basic mechanics addressed above will only help make this process easier. Here we’ll go through the tools you’ll need and the basic process to replace your chain at home.

How often should you replace your chain? Before answering that question, it helps to understand the process of chain wear. As your chain ages, each link’s internal bushings slowly lengthen. In turn, your now-longer chain puts added pressure on your cassette cogs and chainring teeth, causing them to wear faster. This also hampers shifting quality.

To avoid this accelerated wear of your cassette and chainrings, a general rule of thumb is to replace your bike’s chain every 2,000 miles. Mind you, this is just a starting point. No two chains will wear at exactly the same rate because no two riders treat their chains the same.

These differences in riding style are why it is best to periodically use a chain wear measuring tool to determine the condition of your chain. With the tool in hand, apply pressure to a pedal so the top of the chain is taut, and then place the measuring tool in place on the chain as shown in the video above and read the results. Indicators on the tool will tell you whether it’s time to replace your chain.

Cutting a new bike chain to the correct length for installation and removing a damaged link for an on-trail chain repair are essentially the same job. Make life easier by using a full-size tool at home, and save the compact tool for midride fixes.

To start, you’ll need to pick up the right size chain for your bike. We’re not talking about the length of the chain here (you’ll address that later), but width. This is dictated by the number of cogs on your cassette; a six-speed bike uses the same width chain as an eight-speed, but a nine-speed needs something different, and so on. (Check out Park Tool’s chain compatibility guide for more on this.) The easiest way to ensure you get the right chain is to buy the same kind of chain that came on your bike. If you decide to go with a different chain, it’s best to get one from the same manufacturer.

If your chain has a master link such as a Shimano Quick Link or SRAM PowerLock, use a pair of master link pliers to compress the link and undo it. (If it’s a newer chain, you might be able to do this with your hands.)

If there isn’t a master link, remove the chain using the chain breaker tool. Back out the tool’s pin to make room and fit a chain link into the outer slot, and line up the tool’s pin with a pin on the chain. Tighten the tool until its pin puts light pressure on the chain’s connecting pin. Crank the handle, making sure the tool’s pin stays straight. If it twists, stop and realign everything so as not to bend the tool’s pin. If you bend it, most tools have replaceable pins available; some even come with one inside the handle. Then push the pin far enough through so you can remove the extra links.

Remove the chain from your bike. Then, measure out the length of your new chain to match the length of your old chain, taking into account the master link. Remove any excess links from the new chain using the chain breaker tool, and install the master link. Thread the new chain onto your bike’s cassette and chainring and connect the ends with the master link, making sure the link is secure and locked in place.

When she’s not out riding her mountain bike, Jessica is an editor for Popular Mechanics. She was previously an editor for Bicycling magazine.
